0.title: How to Behave in the Household of God
0.overview:
First Timothy is a letter from a seasoned apostle to a young pastor — and it is as practical and urgent as anything Paul ever wrote. Timothy had been left in Ephesus to deal with a crisis: false teachers were infecting the church with 'different doctrine,' with myths and endless genealogies, with a distorted use of the law and a spiritualised asceticism that forbade marriage and certain foods. Paul's letter is his pastoral briefing for a young man who has been given a very hard assignment in a very important city.

Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia — a commercial and religious metropolis, home to the great temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. It was a city Paul knew intimately: he had spent nearly three years there on his third missionary journey (Acts 19–20), and the church he planted was one of the most strategic in the Roman East. Now, years later, that church was in danger. The false teachers were not outsiders; they had come from within — perhaps former elders or teachers who had 'made shipwreck of their faith' (1:19–20). Timothy's task was to confront them, silence them, and restore the church to sound doctrine and ordered life.

The letter's great themes weave together seamlessly. There is the primacy of sound doctrine — 'the glorious gospel of the blessed God' (1:11) — against which every false teaching must be measured. There is the ordering of the church: prayer, worship, the qualifications of overseers and deacons, the care of widows, the honour due to elders. There is the call to godliness — a word that appears more often in 1 Timothy than in any other New Testament letter — the practical Christlikeness that is the goal of all authentic teaching. And there are the five 'trustworthy sayings' (1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Tit 3:8) — compact theological summaries that sound like early confessions of faith, already familiar in the church before Paul wrote them down.

Did Paul write the Pastoral Letters? Many scholars think a later follower wrote them in his name, arguing that their vocabulary and style differ from Paul’s other letters, that their church order with elders and deacons looks later, and that their travels cannot be fitted into Acts. But each letter names Paul as author, they were received as his by the early church, and the church order they describe is simple: plural elders and deacons, which Paul appointed from his first journey (Acts 14:23; Phil 1:1). Differences of style suit an older apostle writing to trusted co-workers on new subjects. And the travels fit if Paul was released from the imprisonment with which Acts ends, as the early church believed, and then travelled again, to Macedonia (1:3), Crete (Titus 1:5) and elsewhere, before a final arrest. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote them, in the mid-60s.

And what was Timothy’s role? Not a bishop of Ephesus in the later sense, but Paul’s delegate, sent with apostolic authority for a time, Until I come (4:13), to correct false teaching and see that qualified elders led the church (3:1–7; 5:17–22).

Above all, this is a letter about the church as 'the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth' (3:15). The church is not a voluntary association or a religious club; it is the family of the living God, called to hold up the truth in a world drowning in falsehood. That is what gives urgency to every instruction about doctrine and order and godliness: the stakes are not institutional but cosmic. The household of God must be governed well — because the God who indwells it is the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords (6:15).

1.title: The Glorious Gospel and the Worst of Sinners
1.overview:
Paul left Timothy in Ephesus to stop certain men teaching a different doctrine: myths, genealogies and confident talk about the law that produced endless speculation instead of love. The law is good, Paul says, when used for its purpose: to convict sinners, measured by the gospel of God’s glory.

Then Paul turns to himself as the proof of that gospel. He had been a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man, and Christ showed him mercy. “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.” If Christ’s patience reached him, it can reach anyone, and the thought breaks into praise. The chapter ends with a charge to Timothy to fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience, unlike two men who wrecked their faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul writes as an apostle appointed by God our Saviour and by Christ Jesus our hope, to Timothy, whom he calls his true son in the faith, wishing him grace, mercy and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Our Saviour, and Mercy Added

The Pastorals call the Father ‘Saviour’ — salvation was his design, as the Son accomplished it — and only the letters to Timothy add ‘mercy’ to grace and peace: compassion for a struggling minister.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A young, unwarlike Timothy (4:12; 2 Tim 1:7) needed the apostolic commission standing behind him.

Now: ‘Christ Jesus our hope’ tells anyone in a hard post where to look when the situation offers nothing to look at.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

Meaning first. 1 Timothy 1 sets out why the letter was written and what is at stake. Paul had left Timothy in Ephesus to stop certain men teaching a different doctrine: speculative myths and genealogies and a misuse of the Old Testament law, which produced arguments rather than godliness (vv. 3–7). The goal of sound teaching, by contrast, is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith (v. 5). The law is good when used lawfully: it exposes and restrains sin, and the list of sins that follows tracks the Ten Commandments (vv. 8–11). Then Paul turns to his own story as the proof of the gospel he guards. He was a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man, yet Christ showed him mercy, poured out grace on him, and made him an apostle (vv. 12–14). That leads to the first “trustworthy saying”: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom Paul is the foremost; his conversion is a showcase of Christ’s patience for all who will believe, and it bursts into a doxology to the King of the ages (vv. 15–17). Finally Paul charges Timothy to fight the good fight, holding faith and a good conscience, unlike Hymenaeus and Alexander, who made shipwreck of their faith and have been put out of the church so that they may learn not to blaspheme (vv. 18–20).

Setting and background. 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus are called the Pastoral Letters, because they are written to Paul’s co-workers about leading churches. After his first Roman imprisonment (Acts 28), Paul seems to have been released and to have travelled again, around AD 62–64. He left Timothy in Ephesus and Titus in Crete to set churches in order. Timothy came from Lystra, the son of a Jewish believing mother, Eunice, and a Greek father (Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5). Paul had taken him on as a young man, perhaps in his late teens or twenties, and he had served alongside Paul for some fifteen years. He was still relatively young (4:12), perhaps timid (2 Timothy 1:7), and often unwell (5:23). The church at Ephesus, where Paul had spent three years (Acts 19; 20:31), was now troubled by exactly the false teachers Paul had warned its elders about (Acts 20:29–30).

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus. Key words. “Apostle” (apostolos, one sent with authority). Although the letter is personal, it is also official. Timothy would read it to the church, and the false teachers needed to know that Paul’s instructions carried Christ’s authority.

By command of God our Savior. Key words. “Command” (epitagē, royal order, decree). Paul did not volunteer; he was commissioned. “God our Savior” is a title characteristic of the Pastoral Letters (2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3; 2:10; 3:4). In the Roman world, emperors were hailed as saviours; Paul gives the title to God alone. It also echoes the Old Testament, where God is Israel’s Saviour (Psalm 106:21; Isaiah 43:3, 11).

And of Christ Jesus our hope. Key words. Christ is not merely the one who gives hope; he is our hope (Colossians 1:27). Christian hope is not wishful thinking but confident expectation fixed on a person who has risen and will return. The Father and the Son together issue Paul’s commission.

To Timothy, my true child in the faith. Key words. “True” (gnēsios, legitimate, genuine, born in wedlock). Timothy was Paul’s spiritual son, probably converted through Paul’s first visit to Lystra (Acts 14:6–20), and genuinely like him in faith and service (Philippians 2:20–22). The word also tells the church: this man is Paul’s legitimate representative; heed him.

Grace, mercy, and peace. Key words. Paul usually writes “grace and peace”; in 1 and 2 Timothy he adds “mercy” (eleos, compassion for the helpless). Grace is God’s favour to the undeserving; mercy is his pity on the miserable; peace is the resulting wholeness and reconciliation. Timothy, facing a hard task, needed all three.

From God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. Key words. One preposition (“from”) governs both the Father and Christ. They are the single source of these blessings, which places Christ on the side of God, not of creatures.

Textual note. Many modern critical scholars doubt that Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters, pointing to differences of vocabulary, church organisation and theology from his earlier letters. But the letters claim Paul as author repeatedly and personally (1:12–16; 2 Timothy 4:9–21); the early church accepted them without question (they are cited or echoed by Polycarp and named by Irenaeus); differences of vocabulary are well explained by different subject matter, a different stage of life, and possibly a different secretary (perhaps Luke, 2 Timothy 4:11); and a pseudonymous letter with forged personal details would have been regarded as a deception and rejected. We receive them as Paul’s, and as Scripture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the letter is merely private advice to a friend. It is apostolic instruction for the church, “how one ought to behave in the household of God” (3:15).

In a sentence. From Paul, sent as an apostle of Christ Jesus by order of God our Saviour and of Christ Jesus, who is our hope, to Timothy, my genuine son in the faith: grace, mercy and peace to you from God the Father and from Christ Jesus our Lord.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for someone who has been a spiritual father or mother to you, or ask him to make you one to a younger believer.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy came from Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, and joined Paul on his second journey. The letter seems to come from after the events of Acts, probably after Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment, in the early to mid 60s AD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Without his usual thanksgiving, Paul gets straight to the problem. He left Timothy in Ephesus to stop certain people teaching a different doctrine and spending their energy on myths and endless genealogies, which breed speculation rather than God’s work, which is by faith. The goal of Paul’s instruction is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith. These teachers have wandered into empty talk, wanting to be teachers of the law without understanding it. The law is good when used properly: it is aimed not at the righteous but at lawbreakers of every kind, at whatever contradicts the sound teaching of the gospel entrusted to Paul.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Teaching Is For

The telos of the whole charge is love (v.5) — Paul is not setting doctrine against love but saying what doctrine is for — and the law, good when used lawfully (v.8), convicts sinners and drives them to Christ rather than feeding speculation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul diagnoses the Ephesian teaching by its output — endless speculation rather than God's household well run (v.4).

Now: The vice list of vv.9–10 must be read where Paul put it: five verses before he calls himself the foremost sinner alive.

verseByVerse.quote: As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.

As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus. Key words. “Urged” (parakaleō, appealed to, encouraged). “Remain” (prosmeinai, stay on). Timothy may have wanted to leave with Paul; Paul asked him to stay in a difficult post. This journey to Macedonia is not recorded in Acts, which supports the view that Paul was released after his first imprisonment.

So that you may charge certain persons. Key words. “Charge” (parangellō, command, order with authority), a key word in this letter (1:5, 18; 4:11; 5:7; 6:13, 17). “Certain persons” (tisin): Paul does not name them yet, perhaps hoping they will repent; some were probably elders of the church itself (Acts 20:30).

Not to teach any different doctrine. Key words. One compound verb, heterodidaskaleō, “teach other things,” from which comes the idea of heterodoxy. Their teaching differed from the apostolic gospel (6:3). The church’s doctrine is not open to endless variation; there is a fixed body of truth, the faith that Jude says was delivered once for all to the saints (Jude 3).

Nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies. Key words. “Devote themselves” (prosechō, pay attention to, be absorbed in). “Myths” (mythoi, fables, invented stories). “Genealogies” (genealogiai, lists of ancestry). The false teaching seems to have had a Jewish flavour (vv. 7; Titus 1:14; 3:9): elaborate speculations built on Old Testament family trees and legends, like the imaginative expansions found in some later Jewish writings. “Endless” (aperantos, without limit, never reaching a conclusion): such speculation goes on forever and never arrives at truth or godliness.

Which promote speculations. Key words. “Speculations” (ekzētēseis, controversial questions, disputes). The fruit of the false teaching was argument and division, not faith and love (6:4–5; 2 Timothy 2:23).

Rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith. Key words. “Stewardship” (oikonomia, management of a household, God’s plan or order). God has a saving plan, his way of running his household, and it is received and carried out by faith. Some manuscripts read oikodomē, “edification” (building up), but the better reading is “stewardship.” The contrast is between human speculation and God’s revealed way of salvation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Old Testament genealogies are useless. They are part of Scripture and trace the line of the Messiah (Matthew 1; Luke 3). The problem was using them as material for fanciful speculation divorced from the gospel. Nor does it forbid careful theological study; it forbids speculation that goes beyond Scripture and breeds quarrels.

In a sentence. When I was leaving for Macedonia I asked you to stay on in Ephesus to order certain people to stop teaching a different doctrine and to stop being absorbed in legends and never-ending family trees, which only stir up arguments instead of advancing God’s saving plan, which works through faith.

On a Tuesday. Notice the topics that absorb your Christian attention. Do they lead to faith and love, or only to argument? Turn from the second to the first.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the leading city of the province of Asia, where Paul had spent about three years.

verseByVerse.quote: The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.

The aim of our charge. Key words. “Aim” (telos, goal, end, purpose). “Charge” (parangelia, command, instruction): Paul’s instruction to Timothy, and more broadly the apostolic teaching he is to give. The point of sound doctrine is not winning arguments but producing a certain kind of person.

Is love. Key words. “Love” (agapē, self-giving love for God and others). This is the fruit of true teaching, in sharp contrast with the speculations of verse 4, which produced quarrels. Love is the fulfilment of the law (Romans 13:10) and the greatest of the virtues (1 Corinthians 13:13).

That issues from a pure heart. Key words. “Issues from” (ek, out of): love flows from three sources. “Pure” (katharos, clean, unmixed). The heart is the centre of the person: thought, desire and will. A pure heart is one cleansed by God (Psalm 51:10; Acts 15:9) and wholly devoted to him (Matthew 5:8).

And a good conscience. Key words. “Conscience” (syneidēsis, inner moral awareness, the faculty that judges our actions). A good conscience is one that does not accuse us, because we have been cleansed by Christ’s blood (Hebrews 9:14; 10:22) and are walking in obedience. The phrase is frequent in the Pastoral Letters (1:19; 3:9; 2 Timothy 1:3). The false teachers had seared consciences (4:2).

And a sincere faith. Key words. “Sincere” (anypokritos, unhypocritical, without play-acting). Genuine trust in Christ, not a show. Paul uses the same phrase of Timothy’s faith (2 Timothy 1:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean doctrine is unimportant so long as people love. Love here is the fruit of sound teaching, not a replacement for it. Nor does it mean love is merely a feeling: it flows from a heart, conscience and faith that God has renewed.

In a sentence. The whole goal of this instruction is love, flowing from a clean heart, a clear conscience, and faith that is genuine.

For worship. Ask God to make your Bible study and theology end in love: to cleanse your heart, clear your conscience in Christ, and make your faith sincere.

verseByVerse.quote: Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion, desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion, desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.

Certain persons, by swerving from these. Key words. “Swerving” (astocheō, missing the mark, failing to aim at the target). “These” are the pure heart, good conscience and sincere faith of verse 5. The false teachers had lost sight of the goal.

Have wandered away into vain discussion. Key words. “Wandered away” (ektrepō, turned aside, as when a limb is dislocated; also used of turning off a road). “Vain discussion” (mataiologia, empty talk, idle chatter). Their teaching was impressive-sounding but hollow, producing words without substance.

Desiring to be teachers of the law. Key words. “Teachers of the law” (nomodidaskaloi), the word used of Jewish rabbis (Luke 5:17; Acts 5:34). They wanted status as authorities on the Old Testament law. Their motive was ambition (“desiring”), not service.

Without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions. Key words. “Make confident assertions” (diabebaioomai, insist strongly, affirm emphatically). They were loud but ignorant: confident about things they did not understand. False teaching often combines great certainty with little understanding.

What it does not mean. It does not mean confidence in truth is wrong. Paul himself speaks with certainty. The problem is confidence without understanding, and teaching for status.

In a sentence. Some have missed this target and drifted off into empty talk; they want to be known as experts in the law, yet they do not understand their own words or the matters they are so sure about.

On a Tuesday. Before you speak with confidence about a spiritual matter, ask: do I actually understand this from Scripture? Humility guards against error.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,

Now we know that the law is good. Key words. “Law” (nomos), here the Law of Moses, the Old Testament moral law in particular. “Good” (kalos, excellent, fine, beautiful). Paul guards against the opposite error: because false teachers misused the law, some might reject it altogether. But the law is “holy and righteous and good” (Romans 7:12). It reflects God’s character.

If one uses it lawfully. Key words. A wordplay: the law (nomos) is good if used lawfully (nomimōs). The law has a proper use and an improper use. The false teachers were using it as a source of speculation, or perhaps as a ladder of merit. Its proper use is the one given in verses 9–10.

Where Christians differ: what is the place of the law for Christians? Some say the Old Testament law has no role for Christians at all; others make it a way of earning favour with God. Verdict: The Reformed tradition, following Scripture, speaks of three uses of the moral law. First, it shows us our sin and drives us to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). Second, it restrains evil in society (the use in view here, vv. 9–10). Third, it guides believers in grateful obedience (Romans 13:8–10; Ephesians 6:2). The ceremonial laws are fulfilled in Christ and no longer binding (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1–14); the civil laws of Israel expired with Israel’s state, though their principles of justice remain instructive. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains God’s will, but it is never the way of justification.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are saved by keeping the law. No one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16). Nor does it mean the law is bad because it cannot save; the fault lies in us, not in the law (Romans 8:3).

In a sentence. We know the law is good, provided it is used for the purpose it was given,

On a Tuesday. Read the Ten Commandments this week, not to earn God’s favour, but to see your need of Christ and to learn how to love God and neighbour.

verseByVerse.quote: understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers, the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,
verseByVerse.commentary:
understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers, the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,

Understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just. Key words. “Laid down” (keitai, is set, enacted, a legal term). “The just” (dikaios, righteous). The law is not aimed at people who are already righteous, as if to make them more so through speculation. Its sharp edge is directed against wrongdoing. Those justified in Christ do not live under the law’s condemnation (Romans 8:1), though they delight in its moral content (Romans 7:22).

But for the lawless and disobedient. Key words. The list that follows is structured. The first six words come in three pairs, describing sin against God, matching the first table of the Ten Commandments: “lawless and disobedient” (those who reject authority), “ungodly and sinners” (those without reverence for God), “unholy and profane” (those who treat sacred things as common).

For those who strike their fathers and mothers. Key words. Now the second table, sins against neighbours, in the order of the commandments. “Strike” (patrolōais kai mētrolōais, literally father-killers and mother-killers, or those who beat their parents): the fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12; 21:15).

For murderers. Key words. The sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13).

The sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality. Key words. The seventh commandment, broadened to all sexual sin. “Sexually immoral” (pornoi, those who engage in any sexual relations outside marriage). “Men who practice homosexuality” (arsenokoitai), a compound of “male” and “bed,” drawn directly from the Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, which forbid a man lying with a male. It refers to same-sex sexual acts, not only to exploitative forms.

Enslavers. Key words. The eighth commandment, theft, in its most extreme form. “Enslavers” (andrapodistai, kidnappers, slave-traders, those who steal people to sell them). The law punished man-stealing with death (Exodus 21:16). Scripture condemns the trade that built so much of history’s slavery.

Liars, perjurers. Key words. The ninth commandment, false witness. “Perjurers” (epiorkoi, those who swear falsely).

And whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine. Key words. The list is representative, not complete. “Sound” (hygiainousa, healthy, wholesome; our word “hygiene”), a favourite term in the Pastoral Letters (6:3; 2 Timothy 1:13; 4:3; Titus 1:9; 2:1). True doctrine produces spiritual health; false doctrine is a disease that spreads (2 Timothy 2:17). Notice that sound doctrine and moral behaviour are inseparable: these sins are contrary to it.

Where Christians differ: same-sex relationships. Some argue that Paul condemned only exploitative or abusive practices, such as pederasty, and not loving, committed same-sex relationships. Verdict: The word arsenokoitai comes from the Levitical prohibition, which concerns the act itself, regardless of the relationship. Romans 1:26–27 describes mutual desire, not only exploitation. Scripture consistently teaches that sexual union belongs to the marriage of one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6). This is held with compassion: same-sex attraction is a real struggle for many, it is not itself the same as acting on it, and all of us stand in this list as sinners. The hope is the same for all: “such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

What it does not mean. It does not single out one sin as worse than all others, or suggest that those who commit these sins are beyond grace. Paul goes on immediately to call himself the foremost of sinners (v. 15). Nor does it mean the law has no relevance to believers; it means the law’s condemning and restraining force is aimed at sin.

In a sentence. We know that the law is not aimed at the righteous but at people who break it and rebel, who are godless and sinful, irreverent and profane; at those who attack their parents, at murderers, at the sexually immoral and men who have sex with men, at people-traffickers, liars and perjurers, and at anything else that opposes healthy teaching,

On a Tuesday. Read the list and find yourself in it somewhere. Then remember verse 15. Speak of sin to others as one who has also been forgiven.
verseByVerse.note: The list follows the order of the Ten Commandments, from the first table (God) to the second (neighbour).

verseByVerse.quote: in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.

In accordance with the gospel. Key words. The standard for judging what is “sound doctrine” (v. 10) is the gospel. The law exposes sin; the gospel announces the remedy. The moral teaching of the law and the good news of the gospel agree: the gospel does not approve of sin but saves from it.

Of the glory of the blessed God. Key words. Literally, “the gospel of the glory.” The gospel reveals God’s glory, his radiant excellence, especially in the face of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:4, 6). “Blessed” (makarios, happy, supremely fortunate) applied to God means he is perfectly happy in himself, complete and lacking nothing (6:15). The gospel is the good news from a God who is himself overflowing with joy.

With which I have been entrusted. Key words. “Entrusted” (pisteuō, committed as a trust). The gospel is a deposit placed in Paul’s hands; he must guard it and pass it on intact (6:20; 2 Timothy 1:12–14). This leads naturally into his personal testimony.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the gospel is Paul’s own invention. It was entrusted to him by God (Galatians 1:11–12).

In a sentence. all measured by the gospel that displays the glory of the blessed God, the gospel that was placed in my care.

For worship. Praise God that he is the happy God, and that the gospel is the overflow of his glory and joy.

verseByVerse.ref: 1:12–17 – Christ Jesus Came to Save Sinners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks Christ for strengthening him and appointing him to service, though he had been a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man. He was shown mercy because he acted in ignorance and unbelief, and the Lord’s grace overflowed to him with faith and love. Here is a saying to be trusted: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul counts himself the worst. He was shown mercy so that Christ could display his patience in him as an example for all who would believe. Paul bursts into praise of the eternal, immortal, invisible King, the only God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Present Tense of Verse 15

‘Of whom I am the foremost’ — not was. Nearness to light shows more dust, not less, and only a man who sees himself so can correct others without contempt.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The persecutor became the pattern (v.16): Christ's patience with him is the outer limit that no later case exceeds.

Now: The doxology of verse 17 comes from a man remembering his own conversion and unable to finish the sentence without worship.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service, though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief, and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service, though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief, and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.

I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord. Key words. “Given me strength” (endynamoō, empowered, put power into). Paul’s ministry was not his own achievement but Christ’s power in him (Philippians 4:13; 2 Timothy 4:17).

Because he judged me faithful. Key words. “Judged” (hēgeomai, considered, regarded). “Faithful” (pistos, trustworthy). Not because Paul had earned it, since he was a persecutor, but because Christ, by grace, made him trustworthy and then entrusted him with the work (1 Corinthians 7:25).

Appointing me to his service. Key words. “Service” (diakonia, ministry). A gracious appointment (Acts 9:15; 26:16).

Though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. Key words. “Blasphemer” (blasphēmos, one who speaks against God): Paul had reviled Christ and tried to force believers to blaspheme (Acts 26:11). “Persecutor” (diōktēs): he hunted down Christians (Acts 8:3; 9:1–2; Galatians 1:13). “Insolent opponent” (hybristēs, violent, arrogant aggressor, one who takes pleasure in hurting others). An escalating list: in word, in deed, in attitude.

But I received mercy. Key words. “Received mercy” (eleeō, passive, was shown pity). The pivot of the verse. Paul deserved judgement; he received mercy.

Because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief. Key words. Paul did not fully know what he was doing: he thought he was serving God (Acts 26:9; Romans 10:2). In the Old Testament, sins of ignorance were distinguished from sins done “with a high hand,” that is, in deliberate defiance (Numbers 15:27–31). Jesus prayed for those who crucified him because they did not know what they were doing (Luke 23:34).

And the grace of our Lord overflowed for me. Key words. “Overflowed” (hyperpleonazō, super-abounded, flooded beyond measure), one of Paul’s “hyper” words. Grace did not merely match his sin; it overwhelmed it (Romans 5:20).

With the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. Key words. Grace brought with it faith (in place of his unbelief) and love (in place of his violence). Both are found “in Christ Jesus,” given through union with him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s ignorance earned or caused God’s mercy, as if ignorance made him deserving. Ignorance is not innocence; Paul still calls himself the foremost of sinners (v. 15). The point is that his sin, though terrible, was not the deliberate, knowing rejection of the Spirit that Jesus calls unforgivable (Mark 3:28–29). Mercy remained possible, and God freely chose to give it. Paul’s conversion was God’s sovereign, effectual call (Galatians 1:15–16), not a response to his deserving.

In a sentence. I give thanks to Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me, because he counted me trustworthy and put me into his service, although I used to slander him, hunt his people and treat them with violent contempt; yet I was shown mercy, since I acted in ignorance and unbelief, and our Lord’s grace flooded over me, bringing the faith and love that are found in Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. No one you know is too far gone for grace. Pray today for the most hostile person you know.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.

The saying is trustworthy. Key words. “Trustworthy” (pistos, faithful, reliable). The first of five “trustworthy sayings” in the Pastoral Letters (3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). These seem to be well-known summaries of truth in the early church, perhaps used in teaching or worship, which Paul endorses with his apostolic authority.

And deserving of full acceptance. Key words. “Full acceptance” (pasēs apodochēs, total welcome, wholehearted reception). This truth is not only to be agreed with but embraced with the whole self.

That Christ Jesus came into the world. Key words. “Came into the world” points to his pre-existence and incarnation (John 1:9; 3:17). He existed before he came; he came from the Father into our world as a man.

To save sinners. Key words. The purpose of his coming: not merely to teach or to set an example, but to save, to rescue from sin and its penalty (Matthew 1:21; Luke 19:10). And to save “sinners,” not the righteous (Mark 2:17). This is the gospel in a sentence.

Of whom I am the foremost. Key words. “Foremost” (prōtos, first, chief, worst). Note the present tense: “I am,” not “I was.” Paul does not merely look back on his past; he sees himself, even now as an apostle, as the chief example of a sinner saved by grace. Mature believers see their sin more clearly, not less (1 Corinthians 15:9; Ephesians 3:8).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was literally the worst sinner who ever lived, as a statistical claim. It is the honest confession of someone who knew the depths of his own heart. Nor does it mean Christ came to save everyone without distinction in such a way that all will be saved; he came to save sinners, and those he came to save he actually saves (Matthew 1:21; John 10:11, 27–29).

In a sentence. Here is a statement you can rely on and should welcome with all your heart: Christ Jesus entered the world to rescue sinners, and I am the worst of them.

For worship. Say this verse aloud as your own confession today, putting your name in place of Paul’s: and then thank Christ that he came for you.
verseByVerse.note: The first of five “trustworthy sayings” in the Pastoral Letters.

verseByVerse.quote: But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

But I received mercy for this reason. Key words. Paul now gives a further purpose of his conversion. God had a reason for choosing such an enemy.

That in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience. Key words. “Display” (endeiknymi, demonstrate, put on show). “Perfect patience” (tēn hapasan makrothymian, all his long-suffering, the whole extent of his patience). If Christ could be patient with Paul, he can be patient with anyone. Paul is the showcase of Christ’s patience.

As an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. Key words. “Example” (hypotypōsis, pattern, sketch, prototype). Paul’s conversion is the template: every later sinner who believes can look at Paul and know that Christ will receive them too. “Were to believe” looks ahead to all future believers, chosen and called by God. “For eternal life”: the goal of faith.

To the King of the ages. Key words. The thought of such mercy lifts Paul into praise. “King of the ages” (basileus tōn aiōnōn, eternal King, ruler over all the ages of history). God rules over every era.

Immortal, invisible, the only God. Key words. “Immortal” (aphthartos, incorruptible, not subject to decay). “Invisible” (aoratos, unseen; no one has seen God in his essence, John 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:16). The only God: there is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). Some later manuscripts add “wise” (only wise God), borrowed from Romans 16:27; the earlier reading is “the only God.”

Be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen. Key words. “Forever and ever” (eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn, to the ages of the ages). “Amen”: so be it, it is true.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only notorious sinners are examples of grace. Every believer is saved by the same patience. Nor does Christ’s patience mean he is indifferent to sin; his patience gives time for repentance (Romans 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9).

In a sentence. Yet for this very reason I was shown mercy: so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus could show the full extent of his patience, as a pattern for all who would later trust him and receive eternal life. Now to the eternal King, deathless, unseen, the one and only God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

For worship. Sing or pray a doxology today to the King of the ages, thanking him for his patience with you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul entrusts this charge to Timothy, in line with the prophecies once spoken about him, so that he will fight the good fight, holding on to faith and a good conscience. Some have rejected conscience and wrecked their faith, among them Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul has handed over to Satan so that they learn not to blaspheme.
verseByVerse.theology:
Which Goes First — Conduct or Doctrine

In verse 19 the conscience goes first and the faith goes down after it; and even the severest discipline, handing over to Satan, is remedial — ‘that they may learn’ (v.20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was to fight by the prophecies once made over him (cf. 4:14).

Now: Shipwreck is what happens when a man keeps sailing while ignoring what his conscience tells him about the rocks.

verseByVerse.quote: This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith, among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith, among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.

This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child. Key words. “Charge” (parangelia), the same as verse 5: the commission to guard sound doctrine. “Entrust” (paratithēmi, deposit with someone for safekeeping). As the gospel was entrusted to Paul (v. 11), he now entrusts the charge to Timothy, who must later entrust it to others (2 Timothy 2:2).

In accordance with the prophecies previously made about you. Key words. When Timothy was set apart for ministry, prophetic words had been spoken about him, perhaps at his ordination when the elders laid hands on him (4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6). These words had pointed him out as God’s chosen worker. Paul reminds him of them to strengthen him.

That by them you may wage the good warfare. Key words. “Wage warfare” (strateuomai, serve as a soldier, fight a military campaign). Ministry is spiritual combat against error and evil (6:12; 2 Timothy 2:3–4; 4:7; Ephesians 6:10–17). “Good” (kalē): noble, worth fighting. “By them”: the remembrance of God’s call strengthens Timothy for battle.

Holding faith and a good conscience. Key words. “Holding” (echōn, keeping, retaining). Two weapons: faith (both personal trust and the content of the faith) and a good conscience (v. 5). They belong together. When conscience is violated, faith soon suffers.

By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith. Key words. “Rejecting” (apōtheomai, thrusting away, deliberately pushing aside). “This” is the good conscience. “Made shipwreck” (nauageō, suffered shipwreck). Paul, who had been shipwrecked several times (2 Corinthians 11:25; Acts 27), uses a vivid image: they deliberately threw overboard their conscience, and their faith broke up on the rocks.

Among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander. Key words. Hymenaeus later taught that the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:17–18). Alexander may be the coppersmith who did Paul great harm (2 Timothy 4:14), though the name was common.

Whom I have handed over to Satan. Key words. “Handed over to Satan” means removing them from the church’s fellowship, the sphere of Christ’s protection, and placing them back in the world, Satan’s domain (1 Corinthians 5:5; Colossians 1:13). This is excommunication: the most serious act of church discipline.

That they may learn not to blaspheme. Key words. “Learn” (paideuō, be disciplined, trained, as a child is trained). Even excommunication aims at restoration. Experiencing life outside the church’s protection might bring them to their senses and to repentance. “Blaspheme”: their false teaching dishonoured God.

Where Christians differ: do prophecies like these continue today? Charismatic and Pentecostal Christians see the prophecies over Timothy as a model for prophetic words in churches today. Verdict: The New Testament prophets belonged to the foundation-laying era of the church, alongside the apostles (Ephesians 2:20), when Scripture was still being given. With the completion of the canon, God guides his church through the sufficient written Word, not through new revelations (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). This is held charitably: brothers who differ often love Christ deeply, and God still guides through his Word, wise counsel, providence, and the inward witness of the Spirit to Scripture. But no word claiming to be prophecy may add to or stand alongside Scripture.

What it does not mean. “Made shipwreck of their faith” does not mean true believers can be lost. Those who finally abandon the faith reveal that their faith was not genuine saving faith (1 John 2:19), and the aim of the discipline was still their recovery. Nor does “handed over to Satan” mean cursing them to hell; it is a remedial step, not a final sentence.

In a sentence. Timothy, my son, I am placing this commission in your hands, in line with the prophetic words once spoken about you, so that, strengthened by them, you may fight the noble fight, keeping hold of faith and a clear conscience; some have thrown conscience overboard and their faith has been wrecked, Hymenaeus and Alexander among them, and I have handed them over to Satan so that they will be taught not to blaspheme.

On a Tuesday. Guard your conscience. When it accuses you, deal with it quickly at the cross, before the rot spreads to your faith.
verseByVerse.note: To hand someone “over to Satan” means putting him out of the church, in the hope that he will be brought to repentance.

2.title: One Mediator, Many Prayers
2.overview:
Paul turns to the church’s gathered life. First, prayer for everyone, including rulers such as Nero, because God our Saviour desires all people to be saved, and there is one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom. Then conduct in worship: men are to pray without anger or quarrelling; women are to be adorned with good works rather than displays of wealth.

Finally the most debated verses: women are to learn, but not to teach or exercise authority over men in the church, and Paul grounds this in creation, not in Ephesian culture. Here, as throughout, the app holds the complementarian reading, respectfully stated, and insists that a restriction on a role is never a verdict on a person’s worth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul makes prayer the church’s first priority: every kind of prayer, for every kind of person, including rulers and officials, so that believers may live peaceful lives marked by godliness and seriousness. Such prayer pleases God our Saviour, who desires people of every kind to be saved and to come to know the truth. Paul grounds this in the heart of the gospel: there is only one God, and only one go-between for God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, who gave his life to set people free, a message announced at God’s chosen time, for which Paul was made a herald and teacher to the nations.
verseByVerse.theology:
‘Desires All People to Be Saved’

Verse 4 has been read as all kinds of people, or — more often in the Reformed tradition — as God's revealed will set beside his decretive will. Either way there is one mediator, and his ransom is a substitute's (vv.5–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Under Nero, the church was told to pray — and give thanks — for kings (v.2; cf. Jer 29:7).

Now: The aim is modest: a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified. Paul thought that enough to pray for.

verseByVerse.quote: First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.

Meaning first. 1 Timothy 2 sets the church’s public worship in order, against the background of the false teaching in chapter 1. First, prayer (vv. 1–7): the church is to pray for all kinds of people, including the rulers who might persecute it, so that believers can live quiet and godly lives. Such prayer pleases God, who wants all kinds of people to be saved, because there is one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all; and Paul was appointed to carry that message to the Gentiles. Second, the conduct of men and women in worship (vv. 8–15). Men are to pray with holy lives and without anger or quarrelling (v. 8). Women are to dress modestly and adorn themselves with good works rather than display (vv. 9–10). Women are to learn, quietly and submissively, and Paul does not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over men in the church (vv. 11–12). He grounds this not in culture but in creation (Adam was formed first) and in the fall (Eve was deceived) (vv. 13–14). And he closes with a hard sentence about women being saved through childbearing if they continue in faith, love and holiness (v. 15). The chapter is about prayer that reaches the whole world and a church ordered according to God’s design.

Setting and background. The false teachers in Ephesus seem to have been exclusive in outlook (perhaps thinking salvation was for a spiritual elite or for Jews), contentious in spirit, and particularly influential among some women (5:13–15; 2 Timothy 3:6–7). They may also have forbidden marriage (4:3). Paul’s instructions answer each of these: pray for everyone, because God’s salvation reaches all kinds of people; stop quarrelling; women are to learn, but not to take over the teaching office; and marriage and motherhood are good. When Paul wrote, the emperor was Nero (AD 54–68), who would soon begin persecuting Christians.

First of all, then, I urge. Key words. “First of all” (prōton pantōn): first in importance, not just first in a list. Prayer is the church’s first priority in worship. “Urge” (parakaleō, exhort, appeal). “Then” (oun) connects to chapter 1: in light of the battle for the truth, the church must pray.

That supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made. Key words. Four words for prayer, overlapping but with different shades. “Supplications” (deēseis, requests arising from need). “Prayers” (proseuchai, the general word for prayer to God). “Intercessions” (enteuxeis, petitions on behalf of others, a word used of approaching a king with a request). “Thanksgivings” (eucharistiai, gratitude). Together they describe full, rich, many-sided prayer.

For all people. Key words. “All people” (pantōn anthrōpōn). No one is excluded from the church’s prayers: friends and enemies, believers and unbelievers, rulers and slaves, Jews and Gentiles. The context, which immediately names kings, shows that Paul means all kinds and classes of people, not least those we might be tempted to leave out.

For kings and all who are in high positions. Key words. “Kings” here includes the emperor. “High positions” (hyperochē, places of authority, prominence): governors, magistrates, officials. Christians were to pray for pagan rulers, even hostile ones, as Jeremiah told the exiles to pray for Babylon (Jeremiah 29:7). Not to pray against them, but for them: for their good, their wisdom, and their salvation.

That we may lead a peaceful and quiet life. Key words. “Peaceful” (ēremos, tranquil, free from outward disturbance). “Quiet” (hēsychios, calm, settled within). Not a life of ease for its own sake, but a setting in which the church can worship and the gospel can spread without hindrance.

Godly and dignified in every way. Key words. “Godly” (eusebeia, godliness, reverent devotion to God shown in life), a keyword of the Pastoral Letters, used ten times. “Dignified” (semnotēs, seriousness, respectability, worthy of respect). The purpose of peace is not comfort but godliness.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should only pray for good rulers, or that praying for rulers means approving all they do. Nor does it mean the church’s goal is political influence. The goal is peaceful conditions for godly living and gospel spread.

In a sentence. My first and chief request, then, is that the church bring requests, prayers, pleas and thanks to God on behalf of everyone, including kings and all in authority, so that we may live calm, undisturbed lives marked through and through by godliness and seriousness.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name, for your head of state, your local leaders, and one public figure you find hard to like. Pray for their good and their salvation.
verseByVerse.note: Christians were to pray for rulers such as Nero, under whom they would later suffer.

parallels.desc: seek the welfare of the city

verseByVerse.quote: This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior. Key words. “This” is the prayer for all people (vv. 1–2). “Good” (kalos, fine, right). “Pleasing” (apodektos, acceptable, welcome). God delights in such prayer, because it fits his own character as “Savior.”

Who desires all people to be saved. Key words. “Desires” (thelō, wants, wills, wishes). “All people” (pantas anthrōpous), the same phrase as verse 1. God is not grudging toward sinners. He is a saving God, whose heart is open to all kinds of people, including kings who persecute and Gentiles whom the false teachers may have excluded.

And to come to the knowledge of the truth. Key words. “Knowledge” (epignōsis, full knowledge, recognition). “The truth” is the gospel (2 Timothy 2:25; 3:7; Titus 1:1). Salvation comes through knowing and believing the truth, not apart from it. This is why prayer and preaching go together.

Where Christians differ: if God desires all to be saved, why are not all saved? Arminians argue that God wills to save every individual equally, and that the difference lies in human free will: God does his part, and each person decides. Universalists argue that, since God desires it, all will eventually be saved. Verdict: Universalism contradicts Scripture’s plain teaching on final judgement (Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). As for the Arminian view, Scripture distinguishes between what God desires in the sense of what pleases him and what he commands (his revealed will), and what he has decreed will happen (his decretive will). God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23; 33:11) and sincerely calls all to repent; yet he has, for wise and holy reasons, chosen to save some and not all (Romans 9:18; Ephesians 1:4–5). Two further points help. First, “all people” in context means all kinds of people, including rulers and Gentiles (vv. 1–2, 7), as “all” often means in Scripture (Titus 2:11; compare Revelation 5:9). Second, God’s desire here is the ground for the church’s universal prayer and preaching: we do not know who the elect are, so we pray for and preach to all, knowing that God is pleased to save through that means. The Reformed view does not make God less loving; it makes him the sovereign author of every salvation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God is frustrated, wishing for what he cannot achieve. God “works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11). Nor does it mean that God’s offer of the gospel to all is insincere; the call is genuine, and anyone who comes will be received (John 6:37).

In a sentence. Such prayer is right and delights God our Saviour, whose will is for all kinds of people to be saved and to come to know the truth.

For worship. Thank God that his saving heart reaches every kind of person, and let that make your prayers and witness wide.

verseByVerse.quote: For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.

For there is one God. Key words. “For” gives the reason for praying for all (vv. 1–4). Since there is only one God, he is the God of Gentiles as well as Jews (Romans 3:29–30), of rulers and slaves alike. He is not the tribal God of one group. This echoes the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4).

And there is one mediator between God and men. Key words. “Mediator” (mesitēs, go-between, one who stands in the middle to reconcile two parties). Sinners are separated from a holy God; a mediator is needed who can represent both sides. There is only one. Not Mary, not the saints, not angels, not priests. Christ alone (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; Hebrews 8:6; 9:15; 12:24).

The man Christ Jesus. Key words. Paul stresses Christ’s humanity, “the man” (anthrōpos, human being). To represent humans, the mediator had to be truly human; to bring us to God, he had to be truly God (Hebrews 2:14–17; John 1:1, 14). He is one person in two natures. He remains a man now, in heaven, interceding for us (Hebrews 7:25).

Who gave himself as a ransom for all. Key words. “Gave himself”: Christ’s death was voluntary self-giving (Galatians 1:4; 2:20; Titus 2:14). “Ransom” (antilytron, a ransom price paid in place of another). The word strengthens the ordinary word for ransom (lytron, Mark 10:45) by adding anti (“in place of”). It is substitutionary: Christ paid the price in our place. This is penal substitution: he bore the penalty we owed, to set us free.

For all. Key words. “For” is hyper, on behalf of. “All” (pantōn) again picks up verses 1 and 4.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Many hold that Christ died for every individual equally, making salvation possible for all, with each person’s decision determining whether it becomes effective. Verdict: In context, “all” means all kinds of people, Jews and Gentiles, rulers and subjects (vv. 1–2, 7), as when Revelation 5:9 says he ransomed people “from every tribe and language.” Scripture teaches that Christ’s death was a real ransom that actually frees those for whom it was paid, not a mere possibility. He laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11, 15), for the church (Ephesians 5:25), for “many” (Mark 10:45). A ransom paid for someone who is never released would be a ransom wasted. This is definite atonement: Christ died with the intention and effect of saving all whom the Father had given him. Yet his death is of infinite worth, sufficient for the whole world, and so the gospel is to be offered freely and sincerely to every person.

Which is the testimony given at the proper time. Key words. “Testimony” (martyrion, witness). Christ’s self-giving is God’s witness to his saving purpose. “At the proper time” (kairois idiois, at its own appointed seasons): at the right moment in history God sent his Son (Galatians 4:4), and now in this age the message is proclaimed (Titus 1:3).

What it does not mean. “One mediator” does not mean believers cannot pray for one another; Paul has just commanded intercession (v. 1). Praying for others is not mediating salvation; Christ alone does that. And “the man Christ Jesus” does not mean he is only a man; he is the eternal Son made man.

In a sentence. For there is only one God, and only one go-between who can bring God and humanity together, the man Christ Jesus, who handed himself over as the ransom price in the place of all kinds of people: that is the witness God gave at the time he chose.

For worship. Come to God today through Christ alone. You need no other mediator. Thank him that he paid your ransom himself.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.

For this I was appointed. Key words. “For this” is the testimony of verse 6, the message of Christ the ransom. “Appointed” (tithēmi, set, placed). God placed Paul in this ministry.

A preacher and an apostle. Key words. “Preacher” (kēryx, herald, one who announces a king’s message publicly). “Apostle” (apostolos, authorised messenger). Paul announces God’s message with God’s authority.

(I am telling the truth, I am not lying). Key words. A solemn assertion (Romans 9:1). Why here? Probably because the false teachers disputed Paul’s mission to Gentiles, or the universal scope of the gospel. Timothy knew Paul’s credentials, but the church needed to hear them affirmed.

A teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. Key words. “Teacher” (didaskalos). Paul’s special calling was to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7–9; Acts 9:15). “In faith and truth” could mean faithfully and truthfully, or teaching the faith and the truth. Either way: Paul’s Gentile mission is itself proof that God wants all kinds of people to be saved.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only apostles may share the gospel. All believers are witnesses. But the apostolic office was unique and foundational, and it has not continued.

In a sentence. And this is why I was made a herald and an apostle (I am speaking the truth, not lying), a teacher of the nations in faith and truth.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is for every nation. Pray for one people group that has little gospel witness.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:8–15 – Men and Women in the Assembly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul addresses conduct in the church’s gatherings. Men are to pray with clean lives, not in anger or dispute. Women are to dress with modesty and good sense, making good works rather than expensive display their adornment. Women are to learn quietly and submissively, and Paul does not allow them to teach men or hold authority over them in the church. He bases this on the order of creation, Adam first, and on the account of the fall, in which Eve was the one deceived. Yet women will be kept safe through bearing children, if they persevere in faith, love and holiness with self-control.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Contested Passage, Read Slowly

The crux of verse 12 is authentein; the ESV and the historic Reformed consensus read it as plain authority, restricted rather than abused, and Paul grounds it in the order of creation (vv.13–14) — an order that concerns function, not worth (Gen 1:27; Gal 3:28).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The braided hair, gold and pearls of verse 9 imported social rank into the assembly; Paul replaces that currency with good works, which nobody can outspend.

Now: Whatever a church concludes about who teaches, a restriction on a function is never a verdict on a person.

verseByVerse.quote: I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;
verseByVerse.commentary:
I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;

I desire then. Key words. “Desire” (boulomai, will, intend, a word of authoritative direction). Paul is not offering a preference but giving an apostolic instruction.

That in every place. Key words. “In every place” likely means every place where the church gathers, all the house churches in and around Ephesus (1 Corinthians 1:2; Malachi 1:11). This is a rule for church gatherings generally, not a local custom.

The men should pray. Key words. “The men” (tous andras), males specifically, not “people” in general. Paul now addresses men and women in turn. Men are to lead the congregation in public prayer. This does not forbid women from praying in church (1 Corinthians 11:5), but it gives men a particular responsibility to lead.

Lifting holy hands. Key words. Standing with raised hands was a common posture for prayer among Jews and early Christians (1 Kings 8:22; Psalm 28:2; 141:2). The emphasis is not on the posture but on “holy” (hosios, pure, devout). Hands lifted to God must be clean from sin (Psalm 24:3–4; Isaiah 1:15; James 4:8).

Without anger or quarreling. Key words. “Anger” (orgē, settled wrath, resentment). “Quarreling” (dialogismos, disputing, argument, or inner doubt). The false teaching had stirred up controversy (1:4; 6:4–5). Men in Ephesus were apparently carrying that into worship. You cannot pray rightly with a heart full of resentment against a brother (Matthew 5:23–24; Mark 11:25).

What it does not mean. It does not require raising hands in every prayer; the point is holiness, not posture. Nor does it mean women never pray in public; it addresses men’s particular failing and responsibility.

In a sentence. So it is my instruction that wherever the church meets, the men should lead in prayer, lifting up hands that are holy, free from anger and arguing;

On a Tuesday. Is there resentment in your heart toward someone in your church? Deal with it before you next lead or join in prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Standing with raised hands was a common posture for prayer.

parallels.desc: the lifting up of my hands

verseByVerse.quote: likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.

Likewise also that women should adorn themselves. Key words. “Likewise” (hōsautōs): as men have a particular temptation (anger), so do women (display). “Adorn” (kosmeō, arrange, make beautiful, from which comes “cosmetic”). Paul is not against beauty; he directs it.

In respectable apparel. Key words. “Respectable” (kosmios, orderly, well-arranged, decent). Clothing appropriate to the gathering of God’s people.

With modesty and self-control. Key words. “Modesty” (aidōs, a sense of shame, reserve, not drawing improper attention). “Self-control” (sōphrosynē, sound judgement, good sense, restraint). Both are inner qualities expressed outwardly.

Not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire. Key words. In the Roman world, wealthy women wore elaborate hairstyles woven with gold, pearls and jewels, which took hours to arrange and announced status. Such display in church would shame poorer believers, distract from worship, and could suggest immodesty. Peter makes a similar point (1 Peter 3:3–4).

But with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works. Key words. “Profess” (epangellomai, claim, make a public declaration). “Godliness” (theosebeia, reverence for God). A woman who claims to worship God should be known not for her outward display but for her good works: kindness, hospitality, service (5:10; Acts 9:36).

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all braiding, jewellery, or nice clothes. Rebekah received gold jewellery from God’s servant (Genesis 24:22), and the bride in the Song of Songs is adorned. The issue is extravagant display, status-seeking, and immodesty. Nor is it only for women; men too must avoid vanity. And it does not mean appearance is irrelevant; it means character matters far more.

In a sentence. In the same way, women should make themselves beautiful with decent clothing, modestly and sensibly, not with elaborate hairstyles, gold, pearls or expensive outfits, but with what suits women who claim to worship God: good deeds.

On a Tuesday. Before you dress for church, ask: will this help others focus on God, or on me? And what good work can I do this week that matters more than any outfit?

verseByVerse.quote: Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.

Let a woman learn. Key words. “Learn” (manthanō, be a disciple, study) is an imperative: a command, not a grudging permission. In first-century Judaism, women were often not taught the law at all; some rabbis said it was better to burn the Torah than teach it to a woman. Paul commands that women be taught. Christianity elevated women as full disciples (Luke 10:38–42).

Quietly. Key words. “Quietly” (en hēsychia, in quietness, calmness, a settled spirit). The same word root as in verse 2, “a peaceful and quiet life.” It does not mean absolute silence (as if women could never speak), but a receptive, peaceable attitude, not disruptive or contentious.

With all submissiveness. Key words. “Submissiveness” (hypotagē, subordination, ordering oneself under). Submission to the teaching and to the church’s order, under the elders who teach. Not submission of every woman to every man, but a recognition of God’s order for the church.

I do not permit a woman to teach. Key words. “Permit” (epitrepō, allow) is present tense: I am not permitting, as my settled practice. “Teach” (didaskō) in the Pastoral Letters refers to the authoritative teaching of doctrine in the church, the work of elders (3:2; 4:11; 5:17; 2 Timothy 2:2). Paul is forbidding women to hold the teaching office in the gathered church.

Or to exercise authority over a man. Key words. “Exercise authority” (authenteō, have authority, take authority, a rare word found only here in the New Testament). Some argue it means “domineer” or “usurp authority” in a negative sense. But the evidence from Greek usage of the period, and the pairing with “teach” (a positive activity), suggest it means to exercise authority, here the authority of elders. “Man” (andros): adult males in the congregation. The two activities together describe the eldership: teaching and governing (3:2, 5; 5:17).

Rather, she is to remain quiet. Key words. Again en hēsychia: she is to have a quiet, receptive disposition, not taking the place of public teacher over men.

Where Christians differ: may women be pastors and elders? Egalitarians argue that this verse addressed a temporary situation in Ephesus (uneducated women spreading false teaching), so that once women are educated, they may teach and lead equally. Verdict: The complementarian view is the natural reading. Paul grounds the restriction not in local culture or women’s lack of education but in the order of creation (v. 13) and the account of the fall (v. 14), which apply to all times and places. The same principle appears elsewhere (1 Corinthians 11:3; 14:33–35; Ephesians 5:22–33), and the qualifications for elders assume men (3:2; Titus 1:6). This does not mean women are inferior: men and women are equally made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27), equally heirs of grace (1 Peter 3:7), and equally gifted for ministry. Women may teach other women (Titus 2:3–5) and children (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), share the gospel, explain Scripture privately (Acts 18:26), serve as deaconesses or in a diaconal role, and exercise a vast range of gifts. The restriction concerns the office of elder: authoritative teaching and governing of the whole church.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women may never speak in church, never pray aloud, never share a testimony, or never teach anyone. It does not mean women must submit to every man. It does not mean women’s gifts are lesser, or that women are more easily deceived by nature. It is about the office of teaching and governing elders in the church.

In a sentence. Women should be taught, with a calm and receptive spirit, accepting the church’s order; I do not allow a woman to hold the office of teaching and exercising authority over the men of the church; rather, she should keep a quiet disposition.

On a Tuesday. If you are a woman, use the gifts God has given you in every way Scripture opens to you. If you are a man in leadership, encourage and train women to serve, and make sure they are well taught.

verseByVerse.quote: For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.

For Adam was formed first, then Eve. Key words. “For” gives the reason for verse 12. “Formed” (plassō, moulded, shaped, as a potter shapes clay), the verb used in the Greek translation of Genesis 2:7. Paul’s first reason is the order of creation: God made Adam first and then made Eve from him and for him as his helper (Genesis 2:18–23; 1 Corinthians 11:8–9). In Scripture, the firstborn carries responsibility for leading. This reason comes from before the fall, so it is not a result of sin or culture, but part of God’s good design.

And Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived. Key words. “Deceived” (apataō, tricked, misled; intensified in the second case as exapataō, thoroughly deceived). Paul’s second reason comes from the fall (Genesis 3:1–6, 13). The serpent approached Eve, bypassing Adam’s headship, and she was deceived. Adam was not deceived; he sinned with his eyes open, which made his sin, if anything, worse (Romans 5:12–19 holds Adam responsible). The point is that in the fall, God’s order was reversed: the woman took the lead, and the man followed. The result was catastrophe. The church should not repeat that reversal.

And became a transgressor. Key words. “Became a transgressor” (en parabasei gegonen, came to be in transgression), stepping over the line God had drawn.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women are by nature more gullible or less intelligent than men. Paul does not say that; and men are deceived all the time (2 Timothy 3:13; Titus 1:10). Nor does it blame Eve more than Adam; Scripture places primary responsibility for the fall on Adam (Romans 5:12; 1 Corinthians 15:22). The argument concerns the order God established and what happened when it was overturned.

In a sentence. The reason is that God made Adam first and Eve afterwards, and that it was not Adam who was taken in, but the woman, who was thoroughly deceived and fell into sin.

For worship. Thank God that his design for men and women is good, and that Christ, the last Adam, has undone what the first Adam and Eve did.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.

Yet she will be saved. Key words. “Yet” (de, but): after mentioning Eve’s transgression, Paul gives hope. “Saved” (sōzō), the normal word for salvation in Paul. “She” at first refers to Eve, and through her to women generally; the change to “they” in the next clause shows he means Christian women.

Through childbearing. Key words. “Childbearing” (teknogonia, bearing children). One of the hardest phrases in Paul. Main readings: (1) women will be kept safe physically through childbirth, though Paul’s word “saved” is normally spiritual, and many godly women have died in childbirth; (2) women will be saved through “the childbearing,” that is, the birth of the Messiah, the offspring of the woman promised in Genesis 3:15, though the article is not clearly emphatic; (3) women will be saved, that is, will work out their salvation and show its genuineness, by embracing their God-given role, of which motherhood is a central example, rather than seeking the role of elder. The third reading fits the context best: the curse on Eve touched childbearing (Genesis 3:16), and the false teachers were apparently forbidding marriage (4:3). Paul says women need not take on men’s roles to be saved; they will persevere to final salvation in the path of godly womanhood, typified by motherhood, if they continue in faith, love and holiness. Reading 2 is also attractive, and the two can be combined: the Child born of a woman reversed the curse, and in him women’s ordinary calling is redeemed.

If they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control. Key words. “Continue” (menō, abide, remain). Salvation is not by childbearing as a work; the conditions are spiritual: “faith” (trust in Christ), “love,” “holiness” (hagiasmos, sanctification), and “self-control” (sōphrosynē, the same word as v. 9). Perseverance in these is the evidence of genuine salvation (Colossians 1:22–23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean women are saved by having children. Salvation is by grace through faith alone (Ephesians 2:8–9; Titus 3:5). Nor does it mean that unmarried or childless women are second-class or cannot be saved. Paul honoured singleness (1 Corinthians 7:7–8, 34). Motherhood here represents the whole sphere of women’s God-given calling, not a requirement for every woman.

In a sentence. But women will be brought through to salvation in the path of motherhood and their God-given calling, provided they keep on in faith, love and holiness, with good sense.

On a Tuesday. If you are a mother, see your work as holy service to God, not a lesser calling. If you are childless or single, know that you are not less in God’s eyes; your calling is just as real.
verseByVerse.note: One of the harder verses in Paul. Suggested readings include: kept safe through childbirth; saved through the Childbirth, the birth of Christ; or saved while fulfilling her calling. It cannot mean earning salvation.
