4.title: A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
4.overview:
The Spirit has warned that some will abandon the faith, following teachers whose consciences are seared and who forbid marriage and certain foods. Paul answers with creation: everything God made is good and to be received with thanks, made holy by God’s word and prayer.

Then he turns to Timothy. Refuse silly myths and train yourself for godliness, which, unlike bodily training, pays out in this life and the next. Do not let anyone despise your youth; be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. Give yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation and to teaching. Let your progress be seen. Watch your life and your doctrine closely, for in this way God will save you and your hearers.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–5 – Some Will Depart from the Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit has warned that in the last times some will desert the faith, drawn by deceiving spirits and teaching that comes from demons, spread by hypocrites whose consciences have been burned numb. These teachers forbid marriage and ban certain foods, though God made food to be eaten gratefully by believers who know the truth. Paul insists that everything God created is good and nothing should be refused if it is received with thanks, because God’s word and prayer make it holy.
verseByVerse.theology:
False Teaching That Restricts Rather Than Permits

The Ephesian error was ascetic — impressive for what it gave up — and Paul answers it not by negotiating but with Genesis 1: everything God made is good, created to be received with thanksgiving (vv.3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Seared consciences are made one over-ruling at a time, through ordinary men saying what they know to be untrue (v.2).

Now: Grace at the table sanctifies a common meal (v.5): neither refuse the gift nor grab it, but take it and say thank you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,

Meaning first. 1 Timothy 4 moves from the truth the church upholds (3:15–16) to the lies that attack it, and then to the kind of minister Timothy must be. Chapter 3 ended with a hymn to Christ: manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, taken up in glory. Chapter 4 opens with the opposite sound, the voice of spirits that deceive. First, the danger (vv. 1–5): the Spirit has warned that some will abandon the faith, led by demonic teaching passed on by hypocritical liars. These teachers forbade marriage and demanded abstinence from certain foods. Paul answers that everything God created is good and is to be received with thanksgiving, because it is made holy by God’s word and prayer. Second, Timothy’s own life and ministry (vv. 6–16): he is to teach these things, nourishing himself on sound doctrine and rejecting silly myths. He must train himself for godliness, which is worth far more than physical exercise because it has promise for this life and the next. The Christian labours because his hope is in the living God, the Saviour of all people, especially of believers. Timothy must not let anyone despise his youth but must be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. He must devote himself to reading Scripture publicly, exhorting and teaching, and not neglect the gift given at his ordination. He must give himself wholly to these things, watch both his life and his doctrine closely, and persevere, for in so doing he will save both himself and his hearers. The chapter that begins with demons ends with a young man reading the Bible aloud to a congregation, and that is the whole strategy of God against the lie.

The setting. The false teaching had an ascetic strand: it treated the material world, marriage and certain foods as spiritually dangerous. This may have mixed Jewish food laws with early Greek ideas that matter is inferior to spirit, ideas that later grew into Gnosticism. The teachers may also have believed that the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:18), so that believers should already live like angels, who do not marry (Luke 20:35–36).

Now the Spirit expressly says. The word is rhētōs: in so many words, explicitly, in plain terms. Paul is not inferring this from general principles or reading the mood of the times. He is reporting something the Holy Spirit has stated, through Jesus himself (Matthew 24:10–12; Mark 13:22), through Paul’s own earlier warnings (Acts 20:29–30; 2 Thessalonians 2:3), and through the prophets of the early church. And the tense is present: the Spirit says. The warning was not spoken once and filed. It still stands, and it still speaks to every congregation that reads it. There is comfort hidden in that. The church has never been taken by surprise by apostasy. Its Lord saw it coming, named it, and told his people in advance, which means that when it happens it is not evidence that he has lost control but evidence that he spoke the truth.

That in later times. The phrase (hysterois kairois, subsequent seasons) does not mean some distant final period at the edge of history. The New Testament treats the whole stretch between Christ’s first and second comings as the last days (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18). The later times began when Christ came, and Paul plainly treats what follows as a description of Ephesus in his own day. The prophecy was being fulfilled in the room where the letter was read, and it has been fulfilled in some room in every generation since.

Some will depart from the faith. The verb (aphistēmi) gives us the word apostasy: a standing away, a defection. “The faith” is the body of revealed truth, the faith once for all delivered to the saints. These are not pagans who never believed, but people who had professed it, sat in the meetings, perhaps taught in them, and then walked away from it.

By devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons. The phrase needs reading carefully, because it says something the church easily forgets. “Devoting themselves” (prosechō) means paying attention to, being absorbed in, the same word as 1:4. “Deceitful spirits” are spirits that lead astray (pneumasi planois), and “teachings of demons” are doctrines whose real source is demonic. Paul does not treat false teaching as merely a human mistake, a clever man reasoning badly. He treats it as having a source behind the visible one. The men in Ephesus were not, so far as anyone could see, occultists. They were church people with opinions about genealogies and diet. Paul says there is something else in the room (2 Corinthians 11:13–15; 1 John 4:1–3). Satan’s great weapon has always been the lie, from the garden onward: he is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44).

Through the insincerity of liars. Note at once that the demonic works through entirely ordinary channels. No possession, no spectacle, no darkened room. “Insincerity” (hypokrisis) is play-acting, the word for an actor behind a mask; “liars” (pseudologoi) are speakers of falsehood. Men saying things they know to be untrue, in a normal voice, in a meeting, wearing the face of piety. The devil rarely appears with horns. He far prefers a pulpit.

Whose consciences are seared. Then the terrible clause. The verb (kaustēriazō) is the one used of a hot iron, and there are two pictures in it, both true. A slave or a criminal was branded, marked as belonging to someone: these consciences carry the owner’s mark. And a wound was cauterised, burned until the flesh no longer felt: scar tissue does not feel. These men have not lost their consciences; they have anaesthetised them, by the ordinary process of going against them repeatedly until the nerve dies. It is the same sequence as 1:19, where the conscience was rejected first and the faith went down after it. It is the letter’s steady warning, and it should be taken personally. Nobody arrives at a seared conscience suddenly. It is done one small overruling at a time, and the frightening part is that by the end it does not hurt.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every error is directly demonic, or that every person who holds a mistaken view is a deliberate liar. Paul is speaking of those who have abandoned the faith and teach against it. Nor does “depart from the faith” mean true believers can lose salvation; those who depart show they were never truly of the faith (1 John 2:19).

Can a genuine Christian be deceived like this? A true believer can be confused, misled for a season, and drawn into error on secondary matters; the Galatians were bewitched for a while (Galatians 3:1), and Peter himself had to be corrected (Galatians 2:11–14). What Christ promises is that his sheep will not finally be snatched from his hand (John 10:27–29). The elect cannot be finally deceived (Mark 13:22): the false Christs would lead them astray if that were possible, and it is not. So the right response to this verse is not anxiety about whether you will fall, but watchfulness: stay close to Scripture, stay in a faithful church, and keep your conscience soft. Those are the very means by which God keeps his own.

How can I tell if a teaching comes from deceitful spirits? Not by how spiritual it sounds or how sincere the teacher seems, because hypocrisy is exactly the disguise Paul names. Ask three questions. What does it say about Jesus Christ: does it confess him come in the flesh, truly God and truly man, the only Saviour (1 John 4:2–3)? What does it do with Scripture: does it submit to the Bible, or add to it, subtract from it, or claim a secret key to it? And what does it do to grace: does it rest everything on what Christ has done, or quietly move the weight onto what you must do or avoid? Teaching that makes Christ smaller, the Bible thinner, or grace conditional is not from the Spirit of truth.

In a sentence. The Spirit states plainly that in the times that follow some will abandon the faith, absorbed in spirits that deceive and in doctrines that come from demons, taught by hypocritical liars whose consciences have been burned numb,

On a Tuesday. Test every teaching by Scripture, however spiritual or impressive it seems: the podcast, the bestseller, the confident voice at the Bible study. And keep your own conscience tender by confessing sin quickly. Pay attention this week to the small things you have learned to overrule: the remark you know was unkind, the figure you rounded in your favour, the thing you watch that you would not watch with your pastor in the room. Nobody sears a conscience in one act. Go to God about the small overrulings while they still sting, because the sting is a mercy.

For worship. The Spirit who warns is the Spirit who keeps. He saw the apostasy of Ephesus before it happened, and every apostasy since, and he told the church in plain words, because the God of truth does not leave his children to be ambushed. Against the father of lies stands the One whose word has never failed, and against every seared conscience stands the blood of Christ, which can cleanse a conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). Spirits deceive; he cannot. Teachers wear masks; he never has. Some depart, but none whom the Father gave to the Son is lost, and the Good Shepherd still calls his own sheep by name.

verseByVerse.quote: who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.

Who forbid marriage. Now the actual content of the false teaching, and it is not what a modern reader would predict. Not licence, but restriction. The verb (kōlyō) means to hinder or prevent. The error at Ephesus was ascetic: a religion of renunciation, marked by what it refused. Register that, because we naturally assume false teaching will be permissive, the sort that lets people do what they want. Paul is dealing with the opposite, and it has been at least as common in church history: the teaching that impresses by how much it gives up. These men taught that marriage and sexual union were unspiritual, which flatly contradicts God’s design. It was God who said it is not good for the man to be alone, God who made the woman and brought her to him (Genesis 2:18–24), and God who calls marriage honourable and the marriage bed undefiled (Hebrews 13:4). Paul will soon tell younger widows to marry (5:14).

And require abstinence from foods. “Abstinence” (apechesthai) means keeping away from. Probably specific foods, such as meat or wine, were treated as impure. Jewish food laws may have been part of it, but the attitude went further: treating material things as defiling in themselves. Behind it lay an old and durable idea, that the material world is the problem and that spirituality means getting free of the body. Marriage and food are the two most bodily things there are, so both had to go. The same instinct produced the teaching Paul attacks in Colossians, do not handle, do not taste, do not touch (Colossians 2:21), and would flower into full Gnosticism in the next century.

That God created to be received with thanksgiving. Paul’s answer is not a compromise about how much asceticism is appropriate. He goes straight to the doctrine of creation. God made food (ktizō, created; Genesis 1:29–31; 9:3), and that single clause dismantles the whole system. If the world is God’s and he made these things deliberately, then refusing them is not superior spirituality; it is an insult to the Giver. And note the purpose he names: God created them to be received (metalēmpsis, a sharing, a partaking). They were made for the taking. Declining a gift is not humility when the gift was made on purpose for you. The proper response to God’s gifts is gratitude, meta eucharistias, with thanksgiving: the same root as the Eucharist, as though every meal were meant to be a small thanksgiving service.

By those who believe and know the truth. “Know” (epiginōskō) means know fully, recognise. Believers who understand the gospel know that Christ has declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15) and that the food laws were a shadow fulfilled in him (Colossians 2:16–17). And there is something deeper here. The capacity to enjoy created things rightly belongs to people who know where they came from. An unbeliever can eat and marry, and often does both with great pleasure; what he cannot do is receive them as gifts, because he does not know there is anyone to thank. The Christian alone can taste the bread and see the hand that gave it.

Where Christians differ: is celibacy holier than marriage? Some traditions require celibacy of clergy, or have treated virginity as a higher spiritual state. Verdict: Celibacy is a gift for some, and can free a person for undistracted service (1 Corinthians 7:7, 32–35; Matthew 19:12). But marriage is equally honourable and holy (Hebrews 13:4). Forbidding marriage to ministers contradicts both this passage and 3:2, where elders are assumed to be married. Neither state is more meritorious before God. The Reformers applied this verse directly to compulsory clerical celibacy, and they were right to: a calling to singleness freely chosen for the kingdom is good; a rule forbidding ministers to marry is not.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid voluntary fasting or personal abstinence for good reasons, such as health, conscience, or love for a weaker brother (Romans 14:21; Matthew 6:16–18). The error is making abstinence a rule that defines holiness.

I am single, and not by choice. Is this verse saying I am missing out on God’s best? No. Paul is attacking teachers who forbade marriage as unholy; he is not saying every Christian must marry or that the unmarried are second class. Your singleness is not a spiritual failure, and neither is your longing for marriage, which is the desire for a good thing God made. Jesus was unmarried, and so, at least in his ministry, was Paul. Bring the longing to God honestly; it is not unspiritual. Meanwhile your life is not on hold: the single believer has real freedom to serve (1 Corinthians 7:32–35), a family in the church (Mark 10:29–30), and the same full inheritance in Christ as any married saint. God’s best for you is himself, and that is not rationed by marital status.

Are there modern versions of this error? Yes, and they rarely use religious language. Any teaching that makes a diet, a regime of abstinence, or a renunciation the mark of the truly spiritual is walking this road: the Christian circle where what you do not eat, drink or own becomes the badge of seriousness; the subtle suggestion that married people are less devoted; the wellness gospel that treats certain foods as defiling rather than merely unhelpful. Self-denial for love of Christ and neighbour is good. Self-denial as a ladder to holiness, or a way to look down on others, is the Ephesian error in modern dress (Colossians 2:20–23).

In a sentence. who ban marriage and order people to stay away from foods that God made so that believers who know the truth might share in them with gratitude.

On a Tuesday. Notice where you are tempted to measure spirituality by renunciation, your own or someone else’s. If you are fasting, keep it secret (Matthew 6:17–18). If someone else eats or drinks what you would not, do not file them lower. And at your next meal, stop long enough to see what is on the plate: someone grew it, God sent the rain on it, and it was made for you to receive.

For worship. Thank God at your next meal not as a habit but with real gratitude: he made this food, and gave it to you. Here is the generosity of the Creator against the stinginess of every false religion. The demons forbid; God gives. The lie says the world is dirty; the Maker says it is good. He set a man and a woman in a garden and gave them each other and every tree but one, and when they took the one, he did not withdraw the rest. He still opens his hand and satisfies the desire of every living thing (Psalm 145:16). And the One who gave the bread is the One who became the Bread, and on the night he was betrayed he took bread, and gave thanks.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.

For everything created by God is good. Paul is quoting Genesis 1, where God looks at what he has made and pronounces it good, six times, and then, at the end, very good (Genesis 1:31). “Good” (kalos) is beautiful, fine, fit for purpose. That verdict has never been withdrawn. The fall corrupted human beings and brought a curse on creation (Genesis 3:17; Romans 8:20), but it damaged the world’s use, not its origin. Matter is not the problem, and a religion that treats the physical as inherently unspiritual is at odds with the first page of the Bible, and with the last, where the new creation has rivers and fruit and a city, and with the middle, where the Son of God took a body and kept it.

And nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. The scope is total, and it is a striking thing for an apostle to write to a church under pressure to be more rigorous. “Rejected” (apoblētos) means thrown away, discarded. No food is unclean in itself (Romans 14:14). But the condition matters and is not a formality: if it is received with thanksgiving. Thanksgiving is what turns consumption into worship. The same meal eaten with gratitude and eaten greedily are two different acts, and Paul’s line is not between the things but between the receivings.

For it is made holy by the word of God and prayer. “Made holy” (hagiazō) means sanctified, set apart for God’s use. Two instruments, and both are ordinary. The word of God is God’s declaration that creation is good and that foods are clean, quite possibly the Genesis verdict just cited, and perhaps also Scripture used in prayers at meals. Prayer (enteuxis, petition, intercession, the same word as 2:1) means thanks before eating. Sit with what that implies. Paul says that saying grace over a plate of food sanctifies it, sets it apart, makes it holy. The most routine act of Christian domestic piety, the one children learn first and adults do on autopilot, is here given a genuinely priestly weight. A common meal becomes a holy thing when it is received consciously from God’s hand, and is eaten to his glory (1 Corinthians 10:31).

The harder way. That is the practical answer to asceticism, and it is harder to live than it sounds. The ascetic refuses the gift and feels holy. Paul’s alternative is not to refuse and not to grab, but to take it and say thank you, which requires you to think about God at the very moment you are most likely to forget him: the moment you are enjoying something. It is easy to remember God in a hospital. It takes grace to remember him at a feast.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anything is acceptable if we say grace over it. Paul speaks of what God created, like food and marriage; sin cannot be sanctified by prayer. Nor does it override love: a believer may choose not to eat something to avoid harming another’s conscience (1 Corinthians 8:13).

Does this cover things like alcohol, or food I struggle with? It covers what God made, received rightly. Wine is among God’s gifts (Psalm 104:15; John 2:1–11), so total abstinence cannot be made a test of holiness. But receiving it with thanksgiving rules out drunkenness, which Scripture forbids (Ephesians 5:18), and the same goes for gluttony with food. If something has become a master to you, it is not being received as a gift, and the loving and wise thing may be to put it down altogether (1 Corinthians 6:12). That is not asceticism; it is freedom. A believer who abstains for that reason, or for a weaker brother, is obeying this passage, as long as he does not turn his choice into a rule for everyone else.

Is saying grace just a habit, or does it really matter? It really matters, and this verse is the reason. Thanksgiving at a meal is not a superstition that makes food safe, and God does not need the words. But by it you confess before him, and before whoever is at the table, that this came from his hand and not merely from the shop or your wages. You are setting apart an ordinary act as worship. If grace has become mechanical, do not stop; change it. Name one thing on the table, or one mercy of the day. Let children hear you thank God for specific gifts, and they will learn that the whole world is his.

In a sentence. Everything God made is good, and nothing should be thrown away if it is received with thanks, because God’s word and prayer set it apart for holy use.

On a Tuesday. Enjoy God’s good gifts today, food, rest, friendship, marriage, with thanks. Joy in creation honours the Creator. Take one ordinary pleasure today, the first cup of coffee, a walk in the light, an evening with your wife or husband, and receive it deliberately from God, out loud if you can. Then notice how different it tastes when it has been given rather than merely taken.

For worship. God looked at all he had made and called it very good, and he has never taken the word back. He is not the reluctant God of the ascetics, grudging every pleasure, but the overflowing Father who invented taste and colour, friendship and marriage, bread and wine, and gave them away. His Son did not despise the world but entered it, ate with sinners, turned water into the best wine at a wedding, and rose with a body that ate fish by the lake. One day creation itself will be set free from its bondage and share the glorious freedom of the children of God (Romans 8:21). Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above (James 1:17), and the Giver is better than all his gifts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By teaching these things Timothy will be a good servant of Christ, nourished on the faith and sound teaching he has followed. He must reject silly myths and train himself for godliness, which is of value in every way, holding promise for this life and the next, unlike mere physical training. This is why Christians labour and struggle: their hope is in the living God, the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe. Timothy should not let anyone despise his youth, but set an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity, devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, preaching and teaching, and not neglect the gift given him when the elders laid hands on him. Watching his life and doctrine closely, he will save both himself and his hearers.
verseByVerse.theology:
Godliness Is Trained For

Godliness is trained for like a body, by repetition (v.7), and unlike bodily training its results survive the body — with value for this life as well as the next (v.8). God is Saviour of all as their preserver, and especially of believers (v.10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Public reading of Scripture came first (v.13) in a church where few could read: read, explain, apply.

Now: A young leader earns respect by being an example where nobody is watching (v.12), and a minister whose progress is visible (v.15) teaches his people that growth does not stop.

verseByVerse.quote: If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed. Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness;
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed. Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness;

If you put these things before the brothers. “Put before” (hypotithēmi) is a gentle word: to lay down, suggest, point out. Not barking orders, but setting the truth before people, as a guide points out the path or a host sets food on the table. “These things” are the truths of verses 1–5: the goodness of creation, the danger of the lie, the gift received with thanks. Timothy’s task is not to innovate, but to serve up what he has been given.

You will be a good servant of Christ Jesus. “Servant” (diakonos) is the same word as deacon, here used in the general sense of minister, and Paul uses it of Timothy the way he uses it of himself. Notice what makes a servant good in this verse: not brilliance, not originality, not a large following, but faithfulness in setting the truth before God’s people. It is a standard any minister can meet and none can exceed.

Being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine. “Being trained” (entrephomenos) is a feeding word: nourished, nurtured, brought up on. And it is present and continuous: Timothy is to be constantly feeding on the truth while he feeds others. A minister who has stopped being fed will shortly have nothing to serve. The pulpit that has become a performance rather than an overflow is running on stored fat, and the congregation will eventually taste it. “Good doctrine” (kalēs didaskalias) is fine, beautiful teaching, the same word God used of his creation in verse 4.

That you have followed. “Followed” (parakoloutheō) means followed closely, investigated carefully, the word Luke uses of his own research (Luke 1:3). Timothy had kept close to sound doctrine since childhood, taught the Scriptures by his mother and grandmother (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:14–15). He was not chasing novelty; he was continuing in what he had learned.

Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. The verb (paraiteomai) means refuse, decline, turn away from. “Irreverent” (bebēlos) is profane, common, without any sense of the holy. And the adjective translated silly (graōdeis) is literally old-womanish: the sort of tale told by the fire to keep children quiet. It is a dismissive phrase, and deliberately so: Paul is denying these teachings the dignity of a refutation. That is a real pastoral judgement and not laziness. Some error should be answered carefully; some should be declined. To argue is to concede that the thing is worth arguing about, and there are teachings whose only power is the seriousness with which opponents treat them. Timothy is not told to defeat the myths. He is told to walk past them.

Rather train yourself for godliness. The verb is gymnaze, the gymnasium word, from which our word comes; Greek athletes trained naked (gymnos), and every Greek city had a gymnasium, Ephesus a famous one. It means the disciplined, repetitive, unglamorous work of an athlete in training. Note the shape of the sentence: refuse that, and put the energy into this. Paul does not merely tell Timothy to avoid a distraction; he gives him somewhere to spend the effort. The false teachers had their own rigorous training, the training of abstinence; Paul calls Timothy to the right kind: Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship and obedience. Godliness, on this account, is not a temperament some people are born with. It is trained for, the way a body is, by doing the same unremarkable things repeatedly, long past the point where they feel interesting.

What it does not mean. It does not mean godliness is achieved by human effort alone. Grace trains us (Titus 2:11–12), and we work out what God works in (Philippians 2:12–13). Nor does the phrase “old wives’ tales” express contempt for older women; it was a stock expression for foolish fables, and Paul honours older women elsewhere (5:2; Titus 2:3–5).

If grace trains me, why do I have to train myself? Because God’s grace does not bypass your will; it works through it. The athlete’s strength is a gift: he did not create his muscles or his lungs. But he still has to run. In the same way, it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure, and that is exactly why you are told to work out your salvation (Philippians 2:12–13). Effort is not the opposite of grace; earning is. You do not train in order to be accepted by God; you train because you already are, and because the Spirit has given you the desire. A Christian who waits to feel holy before he prays will wait a long time. One who prays in obedience finds, slowly, that the Spirit meets him there.

What does training for godliness actually look like? Ordinary things, done regularly. Reading the Bible daily, even briefly, with a plan rather than at random. Praying at a set time and place, using the Lord’s Prayer or the Psalms when your own words dry up. Being in church every Lord’s Day, under the preached Word and at the Lord’s Table, not when convenient but as a fixed point. Memorising Scripture. Keeping close company with other believers who will ask how you are really doing. Practising obedience in the small things: the honest word, the kind act, the temptation refused. None of it is dramatic. That is the point. Athletes do not train by waiting for big races; they train on wet Tuesdays.

In a sentence. If you set these truths before the believers, you will be a fine servant of Christ Jesus, nourished on the words of the faith and on the good teaching you have kept close to. Refuse godless, foolish fables; instead, put yourself through training for godliness;

On a Tuesday. What is your training plan for godliness? Choose one discipline (daily Scripture, prayer, memorising a verse) and practise it this week. Make it small enough to keep and specific enough to check: ten minutes in the Gospel of Mark before breakfast, not a vague intention to read more. And name one thing you will decline, the endless feed, the online quarrel, the speculation that leaves you no nearer to Christ, so that the time has somewhere to go.

For worship. Christ is the true and better servant, the diakonos who came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). He fed on his Father’s word in the wilderness and lived by every word that came from his mouth (Matthew 4:4); he never wasted a breath on myths; he trained in obedience through what he suffered (Hebrews 5:8), and his godliness was perfect. He sets the truth before us still, by his Spirit and through his servants, and the bread he gives is himself. Every hour of our training is upheld by his grace, and every step of progress is his work in us before it is ours.

verseByVerse.quote: for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.

For while bodily training is of some value. Paul continues the gymnasium image and makes a comparison, but read it carefully, because it is not the dismissal it is often taken for. “Bodily training” (sōmatikē gymnasia) is physical exercise, highly prized in Ephesus with its great gymnasium and athletic games. He does not say it is worthless. He says it is of some value (pros oligon ōphelimos, profitable for a little, or for a little while), which is a genuine concession, and one you would not expect from a man supposedly hostile to the body. He has just spent five verses defending food and marriage against people who despised the physical. He is not about to turn round and despise it himself. It may also be a glance at the false teachers’ ascetic regimen, which was its own kind of bodily training, and just as limited.

Godliness is of value in every way. The comparison is one of scope. Bodily training profits a little, for a while, in one department of life. “Godliness” (eusebeia) is reverent devotion to God expressed in daily life, and it is of value in every way (pros panta ōphelimos, profitable for everything). It benefits the whole person, in every sphere and for all time.

As it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come. There is the difference, and it is the honest one. “Holds promise” (epangelian echousa) means it has a promise attached, like a deed. Every athlete knows that whatever he builds will eventually be taken from him; the strongest body on earth is on a schedule. Training for godliness is the only regime whose results survive the body it was performed in. But do not miss the first half of the promise: godliness holds promise for the present life, not only the next. Paul is not offering a religion that pays out solely after death. A life ordered toward God is better now: peace with God, contentment (6:6), wisdom, love and purpose, in the plain sense that self-control beats being ruled by appetite, that a clear conscience sleeps better, that love makes richer company than resentment. And it holds promise for eternity: the life to come, the inheritance, the crown (2 Timothy 4:8). Not that godliness earns eternal life, but that eternal life is promised to those whom grace makes godly.

Progress without inspiration. The practical force is in the word training, which the comparison keeps alive. Nobody expects a body to change through good intentions or a single decision. It changes through repetition, when you do not feel like it, over years. Paul is saying the soul works the same way, which is more encouraging than it first sounds, because it means progress does not depend on inspiration.

What it does not mean. It does not mean godliness guarantees health, wealth and comfort in this life. Paul himself suffered greatly (2 Timothy 3:12). The promise for this life is real spiritual blessing, not freedom from trials. Nor does it mean Christians should neglect their bodies; bodies are God’s temple (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Paul will guard this promise against the false teachers who imagined godliness was a means of financial gain (6:5), but he does not withdraw it.

Should a Christian exercise, then? Yes, and with a good conscience. Your body is God’s creation and the Spirit’s temple, and caring for it is stewardship, not vanity. Exercise can give you energy to serve, clarity to think, and years to love your family and your church. What Paul guards against is the inversion: when fitness, appearance or performance becomes the thing you are really living for, and the hours at the gym are guarded jealously while prayer and worship are fitted around them. The question is not whether to train the body but which training is getting the best of you. Keep the body in its place: valued, cared for, and second.

In a sentence. physical exercise does some good, but godliness does good in every way, because it carries promises both for life now and for the life that is coming.

On a Tuesday. Compare how much time you give to physical fitness, entertainment or appearance, and how much to godliness. Rebalance as needed. Look at a normal week in your diary and ask which kind of training you would win a medal in. Then give one block of time that currently goes to the body, or the screen, to the soul instead, and keep it for a month.

For worship. The body that wins today’s race will be dust, but the Lord who made the body has promised it a resurrection. Christ’s own body was broken and laid in a tomb, and on the third day it rose, never to tire or age or die again. Because he lives, godliness is not a gamble but an investment with a promise attached, signed in his blood. This life with him is already good, and the life to come will be better than anything an eye has seen. The God who gives the promise for both lives is faithful, and nothing done for him in the Spirit is ever wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.

The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. The third of the five trustworthy sayings in the Pastoral Letters (1:15; 3:1). It most likely points back to verse 8, the value of godliness for this life and the next, though some think it refers to verse 10. Either way it is a seal stamped on the truth: this is not a pious hope or an inspiring slogan; it can bear your whole weight.

For to this end we toil and strive. Two hard words. “Toil” (kopiaō) is labour to the point of weariness; “strive” (agōnizomai) is the athletic word for contending in the arena, from which comes agonise. The gymnasium image from verse 7 is still running, and Paul puts himself in it with a plural we. He is not prescribing a discipline he watches other people perform. “To this end” means for the sake of godliness and the life it promises. Some manuscripts read suffer reproach (oneidizometha), but strive is probably original. Christian ministry and Christian life both require exhausting effort.

Because we have our hope set on the living God. There is the fuel, and note that it is hope rather than duty. “Hope set” (ēlpikamen) is perfect tense: we fixed our hope, and it remains fixed. The reason a man will work himself to exhaustion for godliness is that he expects something, and the God he expects it from is alive (zōnti), unlike the one in the great temple of Artemis down the road, whose image could neither see nor hear nor save. The living God acts, sees, hears and rescues.

Who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe. Then a phrase that has caused genuine difficulty. “Savior” (sōtēr) and “especially” (malista, most of all, or perhaps that is, namely) must be read together. It cannot mean everyone is finally saved; this chapter has just spoken of men departing from the faith, and the New Testament everywhere assumes a real division. Nor is especially a way of saying believers simply get a better version of the same thing. There are two main explanations. First, God is the preserver and benefactor of all people, giving life, breath, rain and food to all (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17; 17:25), and he is the Saviour in the full, eternal sense of believers. The word saviour in Scripture covers rescue and preservation as well as eternal salvation, and every breath any human being draws is his gift. Second, malista may mean namely, defining which people God saves: all people, that is, all who believe. Either way, the verse grounds the hope that drives Paul’s labour: God is a saving God, and he saves those who believe. Read the first way, the verse fits its context exactly. Paul has been defending the goodness of creation against men who despised it. The God who feeds and sustains everybody is the same God who saves believers, and it is one generosity running at two depths.

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach universal salvation? Universalists cite this verse to argue that God will finally save everyone. Verdict: The verse itself distinguishes between all people and those who believe, which would make no sense if all were saved in the same way. Scripture plainly teaches that unbelievers will face eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46; John 3:36; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). God is the Saviour of all in that he preserves all, shows kindness to all, and offers the gospel freely to all; he is the Saviour of believers in that he actually rescues them from sin and death forever.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all people will be saved eternally. Nor does it mean believing is a work that earns salvation; faith is the empty hand that receives God’s gift.

How does this fit with God choosing his people? Comfortably. Scripture teaches both that God chose a people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4) and that he is truly kind to all and sincerely offers Christ to all (Matthew 11:28; 2 Peter 3:9). He gives sun and rain to his enemies; he commands all people everywhere to repent; and he effectually draws those he has chosen, so that they believe (John 6:37, 44). The general goodness is real goodness, not a trick, and it is meant to lead people to repentance (Romans 2:4). Election does not shrink God’s kindness to the world. It guarantees that his saving purpose will not fail, and it is why Paul could toil so hard: he knew the living God would certainly save those who believe.

In a sentence. This is a reliable saying, worth embracing wholeheartedly. That is why we work hard and struggle: we have fixed our hope on the living God, who is the preserver and Saviour of all people, and above all of those who believe.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you are actually toiling for this week, and what you are hoping in. If your effort is running on duty alone, it will run out. Lift your eyes to the living God and to what he has promised, and let hope do what willpower cannot. And look at your unbelieving neighbour with new eyes: every good thing in his life, his health, his children, his harvest, is the kindness of the God who also offers him eternal life in Christ. Tell him whose kindness it is.

For worship. Thank God for his kindness to all people, shown in every sunrise and harvest, and above all for his saving grace to you who believe. He is the living God: the idols of Ephesus are rubble, and he still reigns. He feeds the sparrows and the ungrateful, the farmer who curses him and the child who has never heard his name, because it is his nature to give. And to those who believe he gives what no rain can give: forgiveness, adoption, a living hope and an unfading inheritance, purchased by his Son. One generosity runs through the whole world, and at its deepest point it is a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Command and teach these things. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Command and teach these things. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.

Command and teach these things. Two verbs, and the first (parangellō) is stronger than we expect for a young man in a difficult post: to give orders with authority. Both are present imperatives: keep on commanding and keep on teaching (didaskō). Timothy is not merely to suggest or commend. He is to command, because, as chapter 1 established, the instructions were never his in the first place. He speaks as Paul’s delegate, and Paul speaks as Christ’s apostle.

Let no one despise you for your youth. “Despise” (kataphroneō) means to think down on, to look at someone and mentally file him lower. “Youth” (neotēs) is relative: in the ancient world a man under forty could be called young. Timothy was probably in his thirties, which in a culture that gave authority to age was young for the job he had, and the congregation contained older men, some of whom he had to correct and some of whom wanted his role. Note the shape of the instruction, because it is not what it first appears. Paul does not tell Timothy to assert himself, or to remind people of his commission, or to be tougher. Nor does he tell the church to respect him. He tells Timothy to be so obviously worth following that contempt has nothing to feed on.

But set the believers an example. The word is typos, the stamp or die that leaves its impression, the pattern or model (2 Thessalonians 3:9). Authority in this letter is not claimed; it is displayed. Timothy’s life would win the authority his age could not. It is the same logic as Paul’s own night-and-day work at Thessalonica, and the same word he used of it.

In speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity. Five areas, and their order repays attention. In speech (logos): what comes out of his mouth and how it is said, the most public thing about him (Ephesians 4:29; Colossians 4:6). In conduct (anastrophē): the whole visible manner of life. In love (agapē): the goal of all instruction named back at 1:5. In faith (pistis): his actual trust in God, which people can see more than we assume, and with it his faithfulness and trustworthiness. And in purity (hagneia): chastity, moral and sexual purity, especially important for a young man ministering to women (5:2). Purity is the private one, and the last, and the foundation of the other four. They run from the most visible to the least, and the least visible is where it is actually decided. A young minister cannot make a congregation respect him. What he can do is give them nothing to point at, and Paul’s counsel to a man being looked down on is not to fight for standing but to earn it where nobody is watching.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add “in spirit” after “in love.” The earliest manuscripts lack it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean young believers must wait until they are old to serve or lead. Nor does it mean age is irrelevant; the church rightly values maturity (3:6). Godly character can make up for the lack of years.

Is this only for pastors? It was written to a pastor, but the pattern is for every believer. Every Christian is watched by someone: children watch parents, colleagues watch the one they know goes to church, younger believers watch older ones. And the five areas are the same for all of us. The particular word to the young applies widely: a teenager can be an example to his parents’ friends, a new Christian to someone who has been in church for decades. You do not need a title to be a typos. You need a life that has been stamped by Christ, so that it leaves his impression on others.

What if people still look down on me, however I live? Then you are in good company. Some despised Jesus, who was without sin. Paul’s instruction is not a technique guaranteeing respect; it is a way of making sure that if you are despised, it is not for good reason (1 Peter 2:12; 3:16). Keep living faithfully, do not retaliate, and do not try to win standing by louder claims or harsher words. Leave your reputation with God. Over time, a consistent life usually earns trust, but even when it does not, it pleases the One whose opinion finally matters.

In a sentence. Give these instructions and teach them. Don’t let anyone look down on you because you are young, but make yourself a pattern for the believers in what you say, how you live, in love, in faithfulness and in purity.

On a Tuesday. If you are young: let your life speak louder than your years. If you are older: encourage a younger believer rather than dismiss them. Pick the one of the five areas where you are weakest, speech for most of us, and watch it closely this week. And take purity seriously where only God sees: the screen at midnight, the private thought life, the friendship that is drifting somewhere it should not. That is where an example is actually made.

For worship. Christ is the perfect typos. He was the young man despised by the elders of his own nation, and he never once answered contempt with self-assertion. His speech was full of grace; his conduct was blameless; his love went to the cross; his faith in his Father never wavered, even in the dark; and his purity was flawless. Not one of his enemies could convict him of sin. And he did not merely leave us an example; he died for our failures to follow it, and now he stamps his own likeness on us by his Spirit, from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18).
verseByVerse.note: Timothy was probably in his thirties — young for a church leader in that culture.

verseByVerse.quote: Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching. Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching. Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.

Until I come. Timothy’s commission was until Paul returned (3:14). Paul expected to come, but in the meantime the church was not left without what it needed: it had the Scriptures and a man to read them.

Devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture. “Devote yourself” (prosechō) is the same word used of the false teachers absorbed in myths (1:4) and devoted to deceitful spirits (4:1). Everyone is absorbed in something; Timothy is to be absorbed in Scripture instead. “Public reading” (anagnōsis) is reading aloud, and it tells us something easily lost. Most Christians could not read, and copies of the Scriptures were expensive and scarce. For a congregation, hearing the Bible meant one literate person standing up and reading it aloud to everybody, and that is what Paul puts first. Before explanation, before application: the text itself, read out. This is the synagogue pattern carried into the church: Scripture read aloud and then explained (Luke 4:16–21; Acts 13:15). Early churches read the Old Testament and the apostles’ letters (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27). It means Paul assumed the Scriptures were being read publicly in a largely Gentile congregation as a matter of course. A church’s primary act of teaching is letting the Bible be heard.

To exhortation, to teaching. “Exhortation” (paraklēsis) is the coming-alongside word: urging, encouraging, appealing, applying, calling the hearers to respond to what was read. “Teaching” (didaskalia) is instruction in doctrine, explaining what the Scripture means. Read, explain, apply. It is the shape of Christian ministry in three words, and it has not changed in two thousand years.

Do not neglect the gift you have. “Neglect” (ameleō) means to be careless of, to let something lie unused. “Gift” (charisma) is a gift of grace: Timothy’s gift for ministry, especially for preaching and teaching and leading. And the warning tells us that a gift can be possessed and wasted. Paul does not say Timothy might lose it, but that he might leave it in a drawer. Gifts must be used and developed; elsewhere he says to fan it into flame (2 Timothy 1:6).

Which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you. Two things had happened at that commissioning: something was spoken over him (dia prophēteias, through or accompanied by prophecy; the prophecies of 1:18 had identified his gift and calling), and a group of men put their hands on him. The council of elders (presbyterion, the body of elders, the presbytery) did it together, with Paul (2 Timothy 1:6). The laying on of hands was the Old Testament gesture of commissioning, identification and blessing (Numbers 27:18–23; Acts 6:6; 13:3), and here it is the church’s public act of setting a man apart. The gift came from God; the laying on of hands publicly recognised and confirmed it. And note who did it: a council of elders, plural. Timothy’s ministry was not self-generated and not conferred by one man alone. A body of men had publicly identified themselves with him, which is exactly the thing to remember when the job is going badly and a man wonders whether he was ever meant to be doing it.

Where Christians differ: does ordination convey grace? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches regard ordination as a sacrament that confers an indelible spiritual character and power. Verdict: Ordination is the church’s solemn recognition of a man’s gifts and calling, and its commissioning of him to office, with prayer. The gift is from God; the church recognises it. The laying on of hands is a fitting sign, not a channel that transmits grace by the act itself. Scripture names only two sacraments: baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all believers must preach publicly. Timothy had a specific calling. But all believers have gifts to use (1 Peter 4:10). Nor does the role of prophecy here mean new revelation continues today; prophecy belonged to the foundational era of the church (Ephesians 2:20).

How do I know what my gift is, and am I neglecting it? Look for where three things meet: what you are able to do that builds others up, what you find yourself drawn to serve in, and what mature believers around you recognise and confirm. That last is the lesson of this verse: Timothy’s gift was recognised by the elders, not merely self-diagnosed. Gifts are discovered mostly by serving, not by questionnaires: say yes to needs in your church and see where God blesses the work. You are neglecting a gift if you know you have been given something useful to others and have quietly stopped using it, through fear, busyness or resentment. Ask an elder or a trusted friend where they see God using you, and start there.

Why does public Bible reading matter if everyone has a Bible now? Because hearing God’s Word together is different from reading it alone. In public reading the whole church sits under the same word at the same moment, the young and the old, the scholar and the child, and God addresses his people as a people. It also guards the church: when Scripture is read at length, the sermon is held accountable to the text everyone has just heard. Many churches now read only a few verses before a long sermon. Paul put the reading first. Listen to it as God speaking, not as a preliminary, and read it well if you are asked to.

In a sentence. Until I arrive, give yourself to reading Scripture aloud to the church, to urging people to respond, and to teaching. Do not let slide the gift you were given, which was pointed out through prophecy when the body of elders laid their hands on you.

On a Tuesday. Before Sunday, read the passage that will be read in church, so that you come ready to hear. Pray for the one who will read and the one who will preach. And ask yourself honestly whether there is a gift you have let slide: teaching children, hospitality, encouragement, music, administration. Pick it up again this week, even in a small way.

For worship. Value the public reading of Scripture in your church. Listen to it as God speaking. And thank God for those ordained to teach you. Here is the wonder: the God who spoke the world into being still speaks, and he has chosen to do it through the plain voice of a man reading a book aloud to a room. He did not leave his church with a secret, or a ladder of experiences, but with a Word, and with gifts of his Spirit to read it, explain it and press it home. The ascended Christ gave pastors and teachers to his church (Ephesians 4:11), and every faithful sermon is his gift. When the Word is read, the Shepherd is calling his sheep.

verseByVerse.quote: Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.

Practice these things. “Practice” (meletaō) means take pains with, cultivate, think about, meditate on. Give careful thought and effort to all that Paul has said.

Immerse yourself in them. The verb is literally be in these things (en toutois isthi): be found inside them, live there. The old translations had give thyself wholly to them, which catches it. Be wholly absorbed, devoted, given over. Ministry is not a part-time hobby, and godliness is not a weekend interest.

So that all may see your progress. The word is prokopē, the pioneer word: the engineers cutting a road ahead of an army, advancing through rough ground. And Paul expects it to be visible. That is a remarkable thing to say to a minister, and a searching one: the congregation should be able to see that he is a better man than he was five years ago. It also settles something about Timothy’s standing. He is not presented as a finished article who has arrived and now dispenses. He is a man still under construction, and Paul wants the building work on public view. A minister does not need to appear perfect; he needs to be visibly growing. A leader who cannot be seen to be growing is teaching his people that growth stops somewhere.

Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. “Keep a close watch” (epechō) means hold fast, pay close attention to. Two objects, in that order, and the order is the point. His own life first, his character and walk with God; then his doctrine, what he teaches. A man may guard his theology with great care while his character quietly comes apart, and this letter has already shown where that ends: the conscience goes, and the doctrine follows it down (1:19). But Paul will not let it collapse into one either. A sound teacher with an unholy life will destroy his message; a holy man with false doctrine will mislead. Sound teaching from a corrupt man is a weapon in the wrong hands, and character without sound teaching is no use to a congregation. Both, watched closely, permanently. Paul said the same to the Ephesian elders on the beach at Miletus: pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock (Acts 20:28).

Persist in this. “Persist” (epimenō) means continue in, remain in. Not a one-time effort but lifelong faithfulness. Many begin well. The crown is for those who finish.

For by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers. The last clause sounds startling and needs stating carefully. “Save” (sōzō) is the full word. No minister saves anybody; Paul has said there is one mediator between God and men (2:5). What he means is what Scripture regularly means by such language: Timothy’s perseverance in godliness and sound doctrine is the means by which God will bring him and his hearers safely through to final salvation. God saves through means: the faithful preaching of the Word and the believer’s persevering faith. Timothy is not the Saviour. He is one of the instruments, and the instruction is to stay usable.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Timothy saves himself or others by his own works, apart from Christ. God alone saves (v. 10; 1:15). But God uses means: he keeps his people through the preaching of the gospel and their continuing faith. Those who persevere are saved, and those whom God has chosen will persevere, because he preserves them through these means (Philippians 1:6; 2:12–13).

If God guarantees that his people persevere, why warn them to persist? Because the warning is one of the ways he guarantees it. God does not keep his people like parcels in a vault, but like a father keeping a child on a mountain path: he holds the hand, and he also says watch your step. The promise and the command are not rivals. The elect will certainly persevere (John 10:28–29), and they will do so by heeding exactly these exhortations. So if you hear the warning and it makes you watch yourself more closely, that is not a sign you are unsafe. It is the Shepherd’s voice doing what it is meant to do in you.

What does watching my life and doctrine look like for someone who is not a pastor? For your life: a regular, honest look at yourself before God, asking where you are drifting, what you are hiding and whom you are not loving, and confessing it quickly. For your doctrine: knowing what you believe and why, from Scripture, and not absorbing every idea that comes through a feed or a friend. Read a good catechism or confession. Ask questions of your pastor. Belong to a church where both are taught. And do it with others: watching yourself is hard alone, because the log is in your own eye. Give one or two mature believers permission to tell you the truth.

In a sentence. Put your mind and effort into these things and give yourself wholly to them, so that everyone can see you growing. Watch your own life and your teaching closely; keep on at it, for by doing so you will bring both yourself and those who listen to you safely through to salvation.

On a Tuesday. Keep a close watch on yourself and on what you believe. Ask a trusted friend this week to tell you honestly how you are doing in both. And ask yourself the progress question: what can people see in me now that they could not see five years ago? If the answer is nothing, do not despair, but go back to the training of verse 7 and begin again, today, with the Word and prayer.

For worship. The God who saves is the God who uses means, and that is itself a mercy. He could have saved us by lightning; he chose to do it through a Book read aloud, a man who keeps watch over himself, and a people who keep listening. Every sermon that reaches us is a thread in the cord by which he draws us home. And behind every faithful pastor stands the Chief Shepherd, who kept perfect watch over his life and his teaching, persisted to the end, and by so doing saved, not himself, for he would not come down from the cross, but all his hearers who believe. He who began a good work in us will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).

5.title: Honour and Order in the Family of God
5.overview:
The church is a family, and Paul tells Timothy how to treat its members: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity. Then two practical matters. Widows: the church must support those truly alone, but families must first care for their own, and a Christian who neglects his relatives “has denied the faith”. Younger widows should remarry rather than take a vow they may not keep.

Elders: those who lead well, especially in preaching, should be paid generously, and Paul quotes a saying of Jesus as Scripture. Accusations against elders need two or three witnesses, but elders who persist in sin are rebuked publicly. Appoint slowly, judge without favouritism, and remember that both hidden sins and hidden goodness will come to light.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy is to treat the congregation like family. He should not scold an older man but appeal to him respectfully as he would to his own father, and treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with complete purity.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as Household, in Practice

This is 3:15 turned into method: treat people as what they actually are — fathers, brothers, mothers, sisters — which rules out both harshness and a deference that never says anything.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A young leader not taken seriously is tempted to be harsher than the case requires (4:12).

Now: ‘As sisters, in all purity’ gives a relationship rather than a rulebook as the safeguard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.

Meaning first. 1 Timothy 5 applies the truth that the church is God’s household (3:15) to the ordinary relationships and practical problems of church life. It opens with a principle (vv. 1–2): treat the church as family, older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in complete purity. Then it addresses widows (vv. 3–16), the most vulnerable group in ancient society. The church must honour and support widows who are truly alone and devoted to God, but families must care for their own, and anyone who refuses is worse than an unbeliever. There seems to have been an enrolled list of widows, aged sixty or more and with a record of good works, who were supported by the church and served it; younger widows should rather remarry, raise families and avoid idleness and gossip. Finally Paul turns to elders (vv. 17–25): those who lead well, especially in preaching and teaching, deserve double honour, including financial support; accusations against them require two or three witnesses; those who persist in sin must be rebuked publicly; Timothy must act without favouritism and must not appoint elders hastily. A personal word about Timothy’s health interrupts (v. 23), and the chapter closes with the observation that both sins and good works eventually come to light, a reason for patience in judging candidates. It is a chapter about welfare lists, salaries and procedure, and it is full of God: the Father of the fatherless and protector of widows, the Lord who sees in secret, the Judge before whom the angels stand. Church administration, in Paul’s hands, is theology with its sleeves rolled up.

Do not rebuke an older man. The verb (epiplēssō) means to strike at, to rebuke sharply, to upbraid harshly; it is a strong word, found only here in the New Testament. Paul does not say older men never need correcting; he says this is not how it is done. Remember the situation. Timothy is young (4:12), holding an office some older men wanted, in a church with entrenched trouble. The temptation for a young man in authority who is not being taken seriously is to compensate: to assert himself sharply, to be harder than the case requires. Paul takes the option away. Respect for age is a biblical principle: you shall stand up before the grey head and honour the face of an old man (Leviticus 19:32).

But encourage him as you would a father. “Encourage” (parakaleō) is to appeal to, exhort, urge; the word implies coming alongside with a gentle appeal. The correction is real, but the manner is respectful, as a son would speak to his father. You do correct your father, but carefully, and never in public.

Younger men as brothers, older women as mothers. Then four categories, and the frame governing all of them is the family. This is 3:15 in practice: the church is the household of God, so treat people as what they actually are. Younger men as brothers: as equals, with frankness and affection, not as a superior lording it over them. You are frank with a brother in a way you are not with a stranger. Older women as mothers: with honour, gentleness and respect. That is not sentimentality; it is a workable rule with real content. And it cuts against the two failures available to a young leader at once: the harshness that treats the congregation as subordinates, and the deference that never says anything at all. Neither is how families work.

Younger women as sisters, in all purity. The last phrase stands alone and is added to one category only. “Purity” (hagneia, chastity, moral cleanness) is the same word as 4:12. Paul is a realist. A young, probably unmarried minister doing pastoral work with young women is in a situation that has destroyed a great many ministries, and he says so without fuss or embarrassment. His dealings with younger women must be utterly free of any impropriety, in thought, word and action, and of anything that could give rise to suspicion. The safeguard he gives is not distance but a relationship: as sisters. That is the exact instruction, and it is better than a rulebook. A man does not have to invent boundaries with his sister; he already knows what is and is not thinkable. Paul asks Timothy to import that instinct, with protective, brotherly love, which protects the women, protects him, and does not require him to treat half his congregation as a hazard.

What it does not mean. It does not mean older people are never to be corrected; it governs how. Nor does it mean the church replaces natural families; it means church relationships are to have the warmth, respect and purity of good family relationships (Mark 3:35; 10:29–30).

What practical safeguards does purity call for? The family instinct comes first, but wisdom adds sensible habits, especially for anyone in pastoral care. Avoid situations that would be private and unaccountable: meet in an open office or a public place, keep a door ajar, let someone else know where you are. Do not let pastoral conversations drift into emotional dependence; if they do, involve a wise older woman or your wife and step back. Never send messages you would not want read aloud. These are not signs of suspicion but of love: they protect the vulnerable from harm and the church from scandal, and they make sure that a sister is always treated as a sister.

What if an older person in the church really is in the wrong? Then he must be told, but as a son would tell his father. Go privately, not in front of others. Speak with respect: begin by honouring what is good in him, and put the matter as a concern rather than a verdict. Appeal rather than command: ask him to consider it before God. Be ready to listen, because age often sees what youth misses. Respect for age never means silence about sin, and it never means tolerating harm to others; if the wrong is serious, or the person is unwilling to listen, involve the elders (Matthew 18:15–17). The gentleness is in the manner, not in the content.

In a sentence. Don’t come down hard on an older man; appeal to him as you would to your father. Treat the younger men as brothers, the older women as mothers, and the younger women as sisters, with complete purity.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone in your church of a different generation. How would you treat them if they were your father, mother, brother or sister? Treat them that way this week. Sit next to the widower after the service. Ask the teenager how he is really doing. Phone the older woman who has been missing. The church is the only family on earth that includes every age, and it only works if we cross the generations deliberately.

For worship. Here is the wonder underneath this ordinary instruction: God has made us a family. The eternal Son is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11); the Father has adopted us and given us his Spirit, by whom we cry, Abba. Those who had no family have been given mothers and brothers and sisters a hundredfold in his house. And every bond in it was bought with blood. We treat one another as family because, in the deepest sense there is, we are: children of one Father, through one elder Brother, who loved us and gave himself for us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church should honour and support widows who are truly alone and in need. Families must first care for their own widowed relatives; anyone who fails to provide for his own household has denied the faith. A true widow hopes in God and gives herself to prayer, while one who lives for pleasure is dead even while she lives. Paul sets out who may be enrolled for church support: widows over sixty, faithful in marriage and known for good works such as raising children, hospitality and serving others. Younger widows should rather marry, bring up children and manage a home, giving the enemy no opportunity, since some have already strayed. Believing women with widows in the family should support them, so that the church can help those truly in need.
verseByVerse.theology:
Family First, and Why

To neglect one's own relatives is to deny the faith and fall below the decency of unbelievers (v.8); caring for an ageing parent is not a lesser duty but where godliness is practised (v.4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The enrolled widows were intercessors (v.5), and their credentials were a lifetime of unrecorded service (v.10).

Now: Paul's remedy for the dangers of verses 11–13 is not more restriction but ordinary life (v.14).

verseByVerse.quote: Honor widows who are truly widows. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honor widows who are truly widows. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.

The setting. In the ancient world, widows were often destitute. There were no pensions or social security; a woman typically depended on her husband, then on her sons. Property law often left nothing in her hands, and there were few respectable ways for a woman to earn. A widow without family could face starvation or be forced into prostitution. The Old Testament repeatedly commands care for widows and orphans (Exodus 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 14:28–29; 24:17–21). God himself is the one who executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 10:18), a father of the fatherless and protector of widows (Psalm 68:5). The early church continued this (Acts 6:1; James 1:27); indeed its first recorded administrative crisis was about widows being overlooked in the daily distribution. But resources were limited, and some were abusing the system, so Paul gives guidelines. He is not inventing a policy. He is protecting one.

Honor widows who are truly widows. “Honor” (timaō) means respect and value, and here it clearly includes financial support, as in 5:17 and Matthew 15:4–6, where honouring parents includes supporting them. The same word lies behind the double honour of verse 17, which Paul immediately supports with two texts about paying workers. This is a paragraph about the church’s welfare roll. “Truly widows” (ontōs chēras, really widows) are those who are genuinely alone and without family support (v. 5). The phrase is doing the work: the church has limited resources and must direct them where they are most needed.

But if a widow has children or grandchildren. “Grandchildren” (ekgona, descendants). The family has the first responsibility. The church is not the first line of support. The family is.

Let them first learn to show godliness to their own household. “Them” refers to the children and grandchildren. “Show godliness” (eusebein) means practise piety, show reverence. And notice where Paul locates the piety. Caring for an ageing mother is not a lesser, secular duty that keeps a person from spiritual things. It is where godliness is practised; it is the fifth commandment in practice (Exodus 20:12). Godliness begins at home. That is the opposite of the arrangement Jesus condemned, where a man declared his resources Corban, a gift devoted to God, and left his parents unsupported (Mark 7:9–13).

And to make some return to their parents. “Make some return” (amoibas apodidonai) is the language of repaying a debt or recompense. Paul is not appealing to sentiment but to obligation. Parents cared for us when we were helpless; we should care for them when they are. A child who was raised owes something, and paying it back when the parent is old is the settling of an account. This was a widely recognised duty even in the pagan world.

For this is pleasing in the sight of God. “Pleasing” (apodektos, acceptable, welcome) is the same word as 2:3, where prayer for all people was pleasing to God our Saviour. Caring for elderly parents is not merely a social duty but worship. The changed sheets and the hospital visits and the patient repetition of the same conversation are seen, and welcomed, in heaven.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church should never help a widow who has family. Circumstances vary. But the principle is clear: families must not offload their responsibilities onto the church. Nor does it mean families must provide everything themselves without help from others.

Does this mean I must have my elderly parent live with me? Not necessarily. The command is to honour and provide, and what that requires depends on the parent’s needs, your own circumstances, and other responsibilities God has given you, including to your spouse and children. For some families, a parent moving in is the loving choice. For others, good professional care is the wise and loving choice, especially where medical needs are beyond what a family can safely give. What Scripture forbids is not using a care home; it is abandonment: leaving a parent unvisited, unfunded, unknown. Whatever the arrangement, stay involved, contribute what you can, visit often, and make sure they know they are loved.

What if my parent was abusive or neglectful? Honour does not require you to put yourself back under harm, to pretend the past did not happen, or to submit to further abuse. You may need distance and boundaries for your own safety and your family’s, and that is not sin. But even then, the gospel may call you, in ways that are wise and safe, to make sure your parent’s basic needs are met, perhaps through others, and to pray for them. Seek counsel from a wise pastor. God sees the debt you never received, and he is a Father who does not fail (Psalm 27:10). Honouring a parent who did not honour you is costly, and it is one of the places where the grace of Christ shows most clearly.

In a sentence. Give due honour and support to widows who are genuinely alone. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they should learn first of all to put their faith into practice by caring for their own family and repaying their parents, for this pleases God.
